subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
That this House express its opposition to the escalation of the nuclear arms race by any nation and, in particular, its opposition to Canada's participation by testing in Canada any nuclear weapon or nuclear weapon delivery vehicle such as, and including, the Cruise missile.
He said: Mr. Speaker, last evening around 9.30 o'clock I was in the airport in Toronto, having spent a very busy day in southern Ontario. I, as other Hon. Members will recognize from their own personal experience, decided at that particular moment to telephone my home in Ottawa to tell my wife the time I managed to get a flight and the approximate time that I would be arriving home. Somewhat as a surprise to me, my daughter answered the telephone even though it was that time of night. It was a humid evening in Ottawa, as everyone in the city knows. She had trouble sleeping, but she was exuberant and happy to talk to her father. I in turn, as parents will certainly recognize for whatever unique, particular reason at a given time, was delighted to speak to my daughter because she symbolized in her own exuberance in the conversation a sort of warmth, humanity and the possibilities for life that one sees in children, particularly that one sees in a special way in one's own children. I hung up the telephone feeling much better, a much more contented and less tired human being than I was before I called.
I had a unique experience this morning which I would like to share with Hon. Members of the House, obviously having mulled over in my own mind at some subconscious level during the night the subject matter of today's debate. When I awoke this morning I thought of another ten-year-old child. This time she was not a blonde, blue-eyed Canadian ten-year-old by the name of Christine, but I thought back to 1945 in Japan. No
doubt at that time there was in Hiroshima a ten-year old child, perhaps named Sachi, Setsu or Yuriko, just as exuberant and just as full of the promise for life, and quite conceivably she had spoken to her father by telephone at some point on that day. Within seconds, that young, exuberant, dark-eyed, blackhaired girl was blown to smithereens.
[DOT] (DIO)
I relate this to you, Mr. Speaker and Members of the House, because I say with all the depth that I can muster that what is involved in nuclear weaponry is the ultimate possibility that I think mankind, wherever they may live, senses at quite an unconscious level that we may well be involved in the process in this century of taking steps, through our own genius at one level in terms of creative scientific imagination, to create weapons of such devastating capacity that all of mankind could be obliterated. All of the prospects, not only for my daughter obviously but for every child and adult in the world, the kinds of things they might do, the poetry they might write, the architectural leaps of the imagination that they may reveal in terms of contributing to society, the dancing they may do, the songs they may sing, the friendships they may have, may never exist again for mankind.
What is at stake in talks that are now going on in Geneva, and in a more limited but very real way the kind of decision process taking place here in the City of Ottawa in the northern part of North America, will have the most profound implications for the future of mankind. I want to quote Pope John Paul II when he visited Hiroshima in February, 1981. He said:
In the past, it was possible to destroy a village, a town, a region, even a country. Now it is the whole planet that has come under threat. This fact should finally compel everyone to face a basic moral consideration: From now on, it is only through a conscious choice and through a deliberate policy that humanity can survive.
I want to emphasize in particular in Pope John Paul's words the last phrase:
-it is only through a conscious choice and through a deliberate policy that humanity can survive.
We in this country are now at a crossroads. We have a profoundly important decision to make. In my judgment, we can continue to make fine speeches and persuasive, rhetorical arguments about the need for peace and disarmament. They are not to be dismissed because we need talk about peace and disarmament. However, words are certainly not adequate in terms of political life because speeches and rhetoric are not enough.
We can go on talking, or we can put rhetoric aside and make a decision that will take us concretely toward a sane nuclear

June 14, 1983
Supply
policy, which is to say a step toward nuclear disarmament. Surely to God now is the time that we in our own land took the same step toward nuclear disarmament.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
I want to begin the substance of my argument not by merely expressing the moral concern that is appropriate and is, I am sure, felt by Members on all sides. 1 want to underline that concern and the moral implications for the possible obliteration of mankind that is a unique situation in our century in the history of mankind. That kind of moral decision is before us. But I want to face the concrete power arguments, if you like, the legitimately perceived security concerns of the great powers of the Soviet Union on the one hand and the United States of America on the other.
Both sides have legitimate security interests; no one in his or her right mind will deny that. But in my view and in the view of many thoughtful people on this continent and in Europe and Asia, both sides have indulged in practices and argumentation since the Second World War that ultimately are false.
Each time one of the great powers has embarked upon a further escalation of the nuclear arms race, it has used its perceived security interests as the rationale. I think we must be honest and put aside ideology. There is no doubt which side, ideologically speaking, of those broad camps every Member of the House is on. But putting that aside, one must acknowledge a certain legitimacy in the military concerns of each of the great powers. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself has said that in the House on a number of occasions. But surely we ought to be disturbed that when the Russians put in SS-20s, they invariably say they are doing that to counter some perceived American threat of American missiles that are already there, and they use that as a bargaining instrument that they hope will cause the West to embark upon serious negotiations that will lead to disarmament.
The same kind of argument is used by the Americans and indeed has been used by the Government of Canada in the past justifying the deployment of nuclear weapons and, in the present, it is an argument that is being used with reference to the proposed deployment of ground-launched Cruise missiles and Pershing missiles in Europe.
This argument, Mr. Speaker, that is so common to both of the great powers was used in a direct conversation I had with Mikhail Gorbachev, senior member of the Politburo who visited Canada recently and met with the Prime Minister and with the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Nielsen). In a private conversation, he repeated the Soviet argument, which is exactly parallel to the American argument, that they have to escalate in this way, or they have to develop a Cruise, because if they do not the Americans will not come to their senses and so on.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that it is surely time that we recognize that both powers make these arguments and that in the context of existing nuclear strength those arguments do not
now have, if they ever had, any logical validity at all. 1 want to stress that. Such experts in the field from the Soviet Union are not normally free to speak, and we know that, but in the United States the experts in the field, including former Secretaries of Defence, a former head of the CIA, former Rear-Admirals, and the experts in Canada, including George Ignatieff, the distinguished former ambassador to the UN, and retired military people in Canada, all agree that there is a balance of terror in the world. They agree that the Soviet Union has superiority in some weapons but that the United States has superiority in others. One side has a more sophisticated kind of delivery system with some kind of orbital nuclear weapon, and the other side has a different kind of delivery system.
When you take all this into consideration and seriously calculate the total implication, any rational person has to conclude, as the people I have just referred to concluded, that there is a balance of terror now. That is important in the strategic argument and discussions that are going on and it is crucial to the argument that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) has been making and that the Government of Canada has been making.
The point I want to make, Mr. Speaker, is that if the Soviet Union embarks on some kind of madness and we in the West retaliate with nuclear weapons-and there are serious moral questions about that, to say the least-there is absolutely no question of the capacity of western powers and the United States to do that and vice versa. If one side has the deterrent, both sides have the deterrent in terms of existing weapons systems now. Any question about limited nuclear wars or theatre nuclear wars is a particular kind of madness entertained by certain military figures in the United States and the Soviet Union. People whose intelligence and imagination I have a greater respect for acknowledge that this is completely ridiculous. Once the trigger is pulled, whatever the situation, however limited, we are in for a nuclear holocaust. We should have no illusions about that, Mr. Speaker.
Where does the Cruise come into this discussion? I want to say something about the Cruise because that is the subject matter of this debate; that is the entity we are talking about testing in this country. In particular, of course, I am talking about the air-launched Cruise.
What is particular about the Cruise as a nuclear weapon? First of all, all Cruise weapons, ground-launched or air launched, are deadly accurate and are low flying. In addition, they are very small and this makes their existence difficult to verify. Finally, the air-launched Cruise, the kind of weapon that is being discussed for development in this country, has a unique characteristic not common to other Cruises: it has the potential for being a first-strike weapon. When you add that potential to its accuracy, its low-flying capacity and its small size, you are confronted with a qualitative change in the development of nuclear weapons.
June 14, 1983

We are not just talking about another extension of the number of missiles or an increase in megatonnage or what have you; we are talking about a qualitatively different horrific weapon that has the potential for a first strike against the Soviet Union. Or as I understand it-because the Soviet Union is probably doing the same thing-for the Soviet Union to launch a surprise attack on the United States of America with its Cruise missile.
In this context I should like to quote an eminent authority on the seriousness of the Cruise, Mr. Speaker. Mr. William Epstein is the former director of disarmament at the United Nations and just two weeks ago he wrote in an article:
The long-range nuclear tipped Cruise missile is one of the most dangerous and destabilizing weapons ever conceived.
Mr. Epstein went on to emphasize that in his view what was particularly ominous about the air-launched Cruise was its first-strike potentiality. It completely destabilizes the current balance of terror, if you like, that exists between the two superpowers.
The other point I would make in this context is that because of its small size, it can be hidden. If the United States, with our complicity, proceeds to develop and deploy the Cruise, it will make almost impossible-but not impossible-future negotiations for verifiable disarmament agreements. This is precisely because the Cruise will be very hard to detect, whether located here in North America or somewhere in the Soviet Union. Therefore, by proceeding with this now, if we think we are having difficulty at Geneva in terms of what is being discussed, it will perhaps be a "piece of cake" to reach a settlement in the current talks compared to the kind of negotiations which would be required after the two sides develop and deploy a Cruise missile.
I would like to switch now to a related matter, Mr. Speaker, which the Government has talked about with a lot of misleading argumentation, and that is the position of NATO when it comes to the Cruise. I would like to begin with a quote from the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), who is here today for this debate, when she raised a question in the House of Commons on March 24 of this year. She said the following when referring to NATO, and I quote:
-the decision which was taken in 1979 applied to the arms control talks and to the deployment of the Cruise-
That is to say, the ground Cruise.
-and Pershing missiles in Europe only, and had nothing to do whatsoever with the testing of any guidance missile system here in Canada.
The Hon. Member made that assertion and, of course, she had responsibility for Canada at that time and knew what she was talking about. The Prime Minister, in response to the question which was raised by the Hon. Member, agreed and said:
Supply
That is to say that there was no obligation coming out of a NATO agreement at all for Canada to proceed to test, particularly, an air-launched Cruise missile. It is clear in my mind that the decision to test, or to participate in discussions which led to the formulation of an agreement between Canada and the United States pertaining to the air launched Cruise, came as a result of a specific request not from NATO but from the United States of America.

I thank Hon. Members for giving me the extended time. The request, Mr. Speaker, to provide a facility for testing that weapon clearly came from the United States to Canada. I would like to say in this context that the former Secretary of State for External Affairs acknowledged in the House on April 29 last that this was the case. That Minister has never denied, either outside the House or in the House of Commons, that this was the case, that it was a bilateral arrangement made between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States.
However, I regret to say that on a matter as fundamentally important as this, the Prime Minister, as is so often his wont, has attempted to mislead the people of this country. He has systematically tried to confuse the nature of the decision which was made about the Cruise. Time after time he has asserted that if Canada goes ahead and tests the air-launched Cruise, it is somehow intrinsically related to our commitments to NATO. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that this is not the case. The former Secretary of State for External Affairs on the Conservative side, who is in the House today, says it is not the case. The former Secretary of State for External Affairs on the Government side says it is not the case. I say it is time that the Prime Minister of Canada stood up and said it is not the case.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
I would like now, Mr. Speaker, to refer to the Geneva talks. Without sounding Pollyannaish, I am sure 1 speak not only for all Hon. Members of my Party but for all Hon. Members here, and indeed for all people around the world who are watching what is going on, when I say that it has been refreshing to see both the United States and the Soviet Union alter their positions.
[DOT] (U30)
I will not go through the sequence of bargaining stances taken by the two great powers, but the whole world notes that each has recognized the legitimacy of changes made by the other side. There is an apparent kind of realism developing which may lead to some kind of sanity in those talks and could
That understanding is correct-

June 14, 1983
Supply
result in agreements signed between the two great superpowers. But again 1 want to stress, Mr. Speaker, that even if we get agreements in the two series of talks going on in Geneva, as important and positive as that will be for mankind, most Canadians are unaware that such agreements will have absolutely nothing to do with the right of either the Soviet Union or the United States to develop an air-launched Cruise missile. I repeat, whatever agreement is reached in the present talks, either the United States or the Soviet Union would be entitled to go on and develop the Cruise missile.
Therefore, I want now to come to our country's role in this historic process. We are at a turning point. It is not customary for Canadians to think in these terms. We are, after all, a limited power. We are not a great nation when it comes to global considerations in either our economic or military impact on the world. But I say, Mr. Speaker, that we are in a particularly important and unique position because we are part of an alliance and have entered into a bilateral arrangement with the United States concerning the possible testing of the Cruise missile. We can now as a country take a positive moral and yet realistic step towards peace and nuclear disarmament on the one hand, or we can continue in what could be a deadly march towards the ultimate holocaust by making a decision which says we, too, in Canada will play our role in developing the Cruise missile.
In what evidently is the majority of opinion of Canadians from coast to coast, including housewives, miners, loggers, bank clerks, professors, former military personnel, clergymen, farmers and political theorists, a whole cross-section of mankind as represented in our country have made it clear they are in opposition to the testing of the Cruise. Our view in this Party is that we should recognize what those people are saying to us. Sometimes majorities can be wrong, and intellectual honesty compels everyone in this House to say that. But if there ever was an instance when the collective conscience of a nation was expressing itself on the side of truth, it is on the issue of the Cruise missile. The majority is right!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
! want to conclude with these two basic recommendations on behalf of my Party. We should take that small but important step for peace by making it very clear that we will not test the Cruise missile in Canada. In addition, we should exercise a kind of imaginative leadership, appropriate for perhaps a middle power in the world, by taking the initiative to urge the United States on the one hand, and the Soviet Union on the other, to begin immediately to negotiate a complete ban on the testing and development of air-launched Cruise missiles.
The argument we could make to both sides would have much more moral and practical persuasiveness if we have already taken the correct decision ourselves. Therefore when the Minister and the spokesperson for the Conservative Party enter into this debate, I hope they will address this very
practical proposition. If they have arguments against it, we on this side would like to hear what they are.
I began, Mr. Speaker, with a personal reference to my daughter and with a reference to that other ten-year-old who was destroyed many years ago in an instant flash in Japan. Surely to God, Mr. Speaker, it is time for idealism and realism to come together in this debate and make the right choice so that children in our land will be able to develop their capacities and taients and have some joy so that never again will ten-year-olds have their lives snuffed out.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like the Leader of the New Democratic Party to clarify that portion of this rather unusual resolution which reads:
-by testing in Canada any nuclear weapon or nuclear weapon delivery vehicle such as ... the Cruise-
What does he mean "any nuclear weapon", and could he explain to me if anyone in Canada with even a smidgen of authority has ever contemplated, suggested or mentioned testing any nuclear weapon in Canada, if by that he means a nuclear detonation?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: I would be happy to answer the Hon. Member's question. It is a two-part resolution, as the Hon. Member knows. We are asking the House to commit itself to opposing the testing of any nuclear weapon on the one hand- it is a long-range commitment-but on the other hand, regarding the immediacy of the request which has now been made by the Government of the United States to the Government of Canada, we are specifically asking the House to oppose the testing of nuclear weapon delivery vehicles such as, and including, the Cruise missile. I think it is reasonably straightforward but I hope my response has clarified it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: No, that is not the answer I was looking for. To his knowledge, has anyone in Canada with a smidgen of authority ever suggested for a moment that we would be testing nuclear weapons in Canada as opposed to a nuclear weapon delivery vehicle?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Well, I think the answer to that is no.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: I am very curious as to why he bothered putting it in if he was simply not trying to frighten the general public by insinuating someone was thinking of testing nuclear weapons.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
Well, it is in the motion and we did not put it in, the NDP did.
The Leader of the NDP brought up the spectre of the Russians reacting to the development of the Cruise missile by building a Cruise missile of their own with, as seems to be a favourite word of the Leader of the NDP, a potential for striking North America. Surely the Hon. Member is aware that the Russians have been deploying an SS-20 missile every five days for a couple of years now, and at a slightly lesser rate than that in the previous two years. Also, these do not have a
June 14, 1983

potential, but, rather, a capacity to strike North America if they were sighted on the closest Russian soil in eastern Siberia. Why does he worry about the Cruise missile, which does not have the range to get here in the first place-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Air-launched.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: -and, in the second place, when there is something he could worry about a great deal more, the SS-20s, which can reach the northwestern United States?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say candidly that I am a little surprised at the question. I am well aware of the existing weapons of the Soviet Union. They are capable of being used against Canada and the United States, and I am as concerned about that possibility as the Hon. Member.
What I was discussing, in terms of the air-launched Cruise, is that if the Soviets go ahead and develop and deploy it, it will give them the real capacity of launching a strike, with first-strike capacity, which could be devastating because of all the reasons I gave concerning the uniqueness of the weapon, its accuracy and so on. Here we have a qualitative change in the arms race. I would be very interested to hear what the Hon. Member's Party stands for on this matter.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: You will hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: However, this Party is opposed to the development of this kind of weapon by either the United States or the Soviet Union. We would like to see this country showing a little practical and moral leadership in proposing an agreement and helping to facilitate the great powers reaching an agreement in which neither of them develops this horrendous weapon.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Leader of the New Democratic Party-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: It is just that on this particular occasion it is a New Democratic motion, However, I would say to him that I trust that even some of the more senior Members in his Party could recall for him and for many of his younger brethren the attitudes prior to World War II, when the same arguments which he made today with regard to nuclear arms were raised with regard to nerve gases and bacteriological warfare. They were, shall we say, the thrills of the sensational press of the weekend in those days. There was not television. Is he not aware that both sides had those weapons in World War II, but did not use them because they were so terrible? Therefore, how does he feel that appealing only to emotions, and most of his arguments were on emotional sides, will guarantee-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Were Hiroshima and Nagasaki emotional?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING

-that nuclear weapons will be used?

speechtext: To answer very quickly, Mr. Speaker, it would seem to me, although there are some factual inaccuracies in the contention, that the weapons prior to World War II which he described were indeed on both sides. However, with respect, I do not see how that is relevant to the argument.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Oh?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: He went on from there to ask how I would think that emotional arguments would somehow be relevant to bringing about peace or disarmament and so on. That was the thrust of his point. I categorically reject the suggestion that what I offered was what the Hon. Member described as an emotional argument. I am among those who believe that passion and logic can be fused, that we are not disembodied spirits. However, I appeal to the Hon. Member that if he is not persuaded by some kind of emotional concern with the fate of mankind, will he at least do me the service of reading the logic which is embedded in the argument? If he does a little research, he will find all kinds of military experts around the world who agree with me and not with him.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question that I would like to address to the Leader of the New Democratic Party is a request that he outline the attitude of himself and his Party, if they are the same, toward the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the commitments that bind the allies in that organization.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, so far as that is relevant to the debate, I made it very clear. I spoke of NATO's position and Canada's position as stated by his former Secretary of State for External Affairs and by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. MacGuigan). I am making the assumption that the Hon. Member heard my argument. If he did not, and 1 do not say this sarcastically, he could simply read Hansard when it is published. I made it very clear that there is no connection between a Cruise commitment and a NATO obligation.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: Aren't you against NATO?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: If I might ask just one small supplementary question, is the Hon. Member suggesting that Canada withdraw from NATO?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: No, no!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: That has nothing to do with it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING

If I said that there is no connection between a Cruise decision and NATO commitments, it would seem to me, in terms of my old Logic IB, to be a non sequitur to say that this has implications for withdrawing from NATO. It may be that the Hon. Member has taken a more advanced logic course than one of which I am aware.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I want to tell the House that I greatly appreciate the words of the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) in that we all seem to be searching together for the same goal-how to preserve peace. 1 agree with him on that score, but I certainly do not agree on the modality or the means of reaching the objective of preserving peace. When he says that speech and rhetoric are not enough, I agree, because reality is a completely different matter.
I am also very glad to have heard the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) raising the point with regard to the motion itself which, to my way of looking at it-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext: It's dishonest.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
-seems to be very misleading in that it implies that someone or some Government in Canada, the previous Government or the present Government, has considered the possibility of testing nuclear weapons in Canada. No Government of which I know, neither previous ones nor the present one, has found this to be the way our Defence was heading.

Mr. Speaker, needless to say, I am very pleased to be taking part in this debate-first of all, as Minister of National Defence, because in that capacity, I share the reponsibility with Cabinet for ensuring that the sovereignty of our country is both protected and respected, and, with our allies and our various alliances, for maintaining our democratic traditions and our rights and freedoms in this country of ours.

I am also very proud to participate in this debate because, along with many others in the House and I am sure many in the public who are listening to us this morning, we as veterans have been through war. I have been lucky enough to live through and survive one and have been a prisoner of war, like many other Canadians and allies. I know the difference between war and peace, between the misery of war and the comfort and delight of peace; but not just any kind of peace- peace with freedom. This is very important.

speechtext:
NATO's security policy is one of deterrence. Within that policy rests the firm conviction that in a nuclear war there would be no winners. The entire purpose of nuclear weapons is to deter aggression, to deter their use by others. The Cruise missile around which this debate is centred shares that purpose with all other nuclear weapons, that is, to deter aggression. But there is a paradox in the strategy of deterrence which must be recognized. If nuclear weapons are to be useful to deter aggression, they must be credible. To be credible, there must be confidence, especially on the part of the opposition, that is the other side, that they will work.
Deterrence is not an attractive way of ensuring peace but it has worked. For it to work, NATO must possess the means to respond to aggression, both conventional and nuclear. The maintenance of a credible deterrent has helped to make western Europe strong and to keep the peace between East and West for over 30 years, despite circumstances that were often very difficult. It is hard to think of any other period in European history where such political divisions and so many potential flash points would not have led to war. That deterrent posture of the West still keeps the peace today.
Deterrence also provides the necessary stability to enable us to pursue arms control measures which will really give us a safer world if they are verifiable and apply equally to both sides. The posssession of nuclear weapons is an essential fact of deterrence. In a world where such weapons exist the NATO alliance must be able to deter their use by an enemy or to resist blackmail based on the threat of nuclear attack. Moreover, the possibility that nuclear weapons might be used remains a valuable disincentive even to conventional aggression against a power possessing them.
By the way, Mr. Speaker, do you think for one minute that if Afghanistan had been a nuclear power Soviet Russia would have invaded it? I think nuclear possession by Afghanistan would have been an absolute deterrent to such invasion.
Since 1945 conventional war in other parts of the world has killed over ten million people, and more are being killed with each passing day. Not only has nuclear war between East and West been avoided, but so also has conventional war in Europe been prevented. Nuclear war is a terrible threat; conventional war a terrible reality.
The crux of the debate is the validity of the strategy of deterrence. The ethical questions raised are grave and difficult. Churchmen and laymen alike are divided by the problem. It is argued that the indiscriminate mass killing associated with nuclear weapons is invariably and absolutely wrong. Therefore deterrence is wrong, some people say. But nuclear weapons exist and they cannot be disinvented.
I noted the Leader of the New Democratic Party quoted Pope John Paul. Let me quote what Pope John Paul said last June in his message to the United Nations special session on disarmament. He attacked the arms race but called for the mutual, progressive and verifiable reduction of armaments. He emphasized that negotiation was still the only realistic response to the threat of war. On the subject now at the centre of the Christian debate he said that: in current conditions
Supply
deterrence based on balance, should certainly not be seen as an end in itself but as a step on the way to progressive disarmament, may still be judged morally acceptable. The Pope commented to anti-nuclear groups that there is a profound and sincere desire for peace but noted that their project proposal and policy can often lend themselves to political exploitation. 1 think what Pope John Paul has said is indeed something on which we should reflect.
There is as well a second morality at issue. Deterrence can be made and kept as a stable system, with only a remote chance of nuclear war. The primary intention is not to kill the enemy but to keep the peace. The question is: Does the immorality of something which will only happen in extreme circumstances outweigh the morality of what is being achieved day by day, and has been achieved for over 34 years, peace in Europe? Surely the greater good is served by ensuring that nuclear weapons are never used by preventing nuclear war in the first place.
Many Hon. Members will have followed the discussion at the recent Anglican General Synod in England on the morality of deterrence. One-sided disarmament, which is indeed what this motion calls for

-was turned down by more than three to one. I think it is unilateral because the Hon. Member only spoke about the West. He never spoke about the other side. Instead, the church called upon the British Government to sustain their nuclear deterrent while seeking multilateral disarmament. We, too, are convinced of the correctness of this multilateral approach. In the meantime deterrence, although perhaps morally flawed for some, is the only means at present whereby war can be prevented and the threat of war kept as it is now, very low. Clearly it is the lesser evil.
Of course, that is not the end of it. No one can rest comfortably on such a policy alone as the basis of international peace for the rest of time. This is why we have to search unremittingly for better ways of ensuring a stable world. Vital among these is the Government's commitment to pursue effective measures of arms control and disarmament. In the meantime, for deterrence to remain effective Canada and other NATO nations must from time to time modernize their defence equipment, as existing systems become obsolete, if they want to retain a deterrent capability.
To those people who imply that Canada believes in building up a western nuclear war fighting capacity, I would like to say that the Government, together with other alliance governments, sees every part of our security policy and every weapon in the alliance arsenal as having only one purpose, that of contributing to deterrence and preventing war. A military balance is essential in today's world to our own security and that of our allies. We must use it as the basis for arms control, not as the starting point for an arms race. We want a balance,

June 14, 1983
Supply
but we want one at much lower levels of armament on both sides than is the case at present.
Of course, that has long been the basis of NATO policy. It was the entire basis for NATO's December, 1979 two-track decision. Canada supported that decision and continues to support its implementation on both tracks, including deployment if arms control negotiations fail to yield satisfactory results. Our deepest wish is that deployment will not be necessary. But in logic it is difficult to see how, if Canadian support for the NATO decision was not then regarded as contributing to nuclear proliferation or to the arms race, any possible assistance with the testing of one of the delivery vehicles could be so construed now.
I recognize that there is a widespread climate of uncertainty, and in some cases fear and insecurity seems to have spread in recent years in the West. Sadly some Canadians seem determined to cultivate that fear and insecurity. They would even have us believe that they have the monopoly on concern for humanity. Of course they have no such monopoly. The Government shares the same concern, at least to as great a degree. We respect those who work for peace, but we reject the sanctimony of those who take unto themselves the word "peace" as if it were their own. We are convinced that Canada and Canadians are best served by a prudent defence strategy and a realistic arms control policy. Within the NATO alliance we have both.
The upsurge of anti-nuclear sentiment, with its overtone of anti-Americanism, is one of the most important problems we face today. The United States has been and remains essential to our security and that of Europe. NATO policies and determination have brought about changes in Soviet attitudes, not those of the peace movements or the unilateralists. It is NATO which is proposing radical solutions in arms negotiations and the Soviet Union which is holding things up. Popular protest should be directed at the Soviet Union, not at the United States. If one had only two choices, to live in one or the other country as a pacifist, which one would be chosen-to live in the United States with its freedoms or in Soviet Russia which incarcerates pacifists or anyone who wants to petition their Government?

Perhaps we have only ourselves to blame. We had assumed that our security policy and the basis for it was both well understood and accepted by the great majority of Canadians. But we may have failed to put over to some the basic aims of the strategy of deterrence-the maintenance of peace as well as freedom. We and everyone listening to my comments are horrified by any prospect of war, but responsible governments have an obligation to face up to the horror of war and work to prevent it. That is what our security policy is about.
Quite frankly, such a motion from a Party that proposes that Canada withdraw from NATO and end our alliance with the Americans does not surprise me. Their ideas on Canadian
defence policy or the lack of it in most areas are well known to the Canadian people. It is more or less a policy of submission. Canadians are overwhelmingly in favour of NATO and our alliance partnerships. The Government will continue its current policy direction so that the freedom, security and peace of all Canadians are maintained.
To do otherwise would be to invite aggression. 1 am thankful that ideas and solutions such as those proffered by Hon. Members of the New Democratic Party did not carry the day in the 1940s in England when the liberty of all the free world was at stake. We on this side of the House have learned from history. I suggest Hon. Members opposite spend a little more time reading and pondering the hard lessons of the past. I could give them a few lessons from my own experiences.

member of the Privy Council. However, 1 would like to point out that the New Democratic Party has never stood and I hope will never stand for any kind of unilateral disarmament.
I say sincerely to the Minister that I think the matter is cheapened when it is put to the issue of choosing whether we would rather be under Soviet control or American control. As an individual I believe, as do Hon. Members of the NDP across the country, in the freedoms and justices for which people like the Minister of National Defence and other Members of the House of Commons fought during the Second World War and during other wars in which Canada has been involved. I do not want to see this debate cheapened to an issue of politics choosing either a communist or free world. 1 believe all Members of this House would choose the free world in which we live, which we would go to arms again for under similar circumstances. I am sure Members would take up that call.

It is not an issue of the United States versus the Soviet Union. It is not an issue of New Democrats versus Conservatives versus Liberals. The question is nuclear arms. This House of Commons and this Parliament should deal very seriously with that issue. The consequences are devastating. Although the Minister mentioned that the Pope had taken an initial step, we must take steps beyond that to work for some kind of multilateral disarmament around the world. Canada can play a very key role in that. I want to set the record straight.

So far, something else has arisen out of these speeches. Disregarding how Members of the NDP have taken this very, very serious subject and have tried to turn it into a political brownie point for themselves, I would like to point out that, by my understanding, today is the final Opposition Day before we rise for the summer. Today is the last Opposition Day with a vote of non-confidence and we are not touching upon employment, we are not touching upon the economy, we are not touching upon things that are important to the people. We are only touching upon this issue that is important to considerably fewer people than the number of people who are interested in unemployment and in knowing from where they will get their next meal.
Recently I sent out a questionnaire to my constituents to which I received 5,000 responses. I realize the bias that is created by questionnaires with questions that are improperly phrased and I also realize that the people who answered my questionnaire are, to a large degree, people who support me. However, the third question on the questionnaire read: "Do you believe Canada should remain in NATO?" I like to keep these questions short because I do not like to influence people. The responses were yes, 86.6 per cent; no, 7.5 per cent; and no answer, 5.9 per cent. The fourth question read: "Do you believe Canada should agree to have the Cruise missile tested at Cold Lake provided no nuclear armaments are carried into Canada during the tests?" The responses were yes, 72 per cent; no, 23 per cent; and no answer, 4 per cent.
Now, to me, the answers to these two questions were particularly interesting when considered within the context of the answer to the eighth question: "Thinking of federal politics only, do you generally consider yourself to be a supporter of the Liberal Party, the NDP or the PC Party?" The responses were Liberal, 7.3 per cent; NDP, 7.3 per cent; and PC, 73.2 per cent. There were 609 responses that did not answer that question.
Now, in actual figures that comes out to 364 people who claim that they are NDP supporters.

Before I go to the main body of my speech, I would like to mention the theological background of this question. For a while this morning, I began to feel as if I were at some kind of a theological college where people were questioning what the General Synod of the Church of England said. A headline from the London Times of Friday, February 11, reads: "General Synod rejects unilateral nuclear disarmament". The article went on to say that unilateral nuclear disarmament was rejected and support given in principle to a British nuclear deterrence. The Synod called for a British commitment to no first use.
Along this theological vein, I read further and found a quotation from Pope John Paul who was mentioned by the Leader of the New Democratic Party. An article in The Economist said that Pope John Paul attacked the arms race and called for mutual, progressive and verifiable reductions of armaments. That is exactly what the Conservative Party called for. The article continues:
Negotiation was still, he emphasized, the only realistic response to the threat of war. On the subject now at the centre of the Christian debate, he said:
"In current conditions, deterrence based on balance, certainly not as an end in itself but as a step on the way towards a progressive disarmament, may still be judged morally acceptable".
The article also had this to say:
Inconveniently, Christianity's founder left behind a less than wholly clear set of rules. He instructed his followers to love their enemies, not to resist evil and, when struck, to turn the other cheek. (Matthew 5:39-44). In the Sermon on the Mount, he praised the peacemakers (Matthew 5:9). Yet he also whipped the traders and the money-changers out of the Temple (John 2:14-16), and rather ambiguously said he had come into the world "not to send peace but a sword" (Matthew 10:34). What were his followers to do?
What his followers do 2,000 years later, I suppose, is to debate the thing to some degree. I would ask that the debate be as informed as possible.
I am pleased that this motion is before the House because we have needed one, Mr. Speaker. I wanted to have a debate after we got the information that 1 have detailed today. I want to point out some of the misconceptions and some of the

misinformation that seems to be abroad in the country concerning the Cruise missile. In view of the number of misconceptions, perhaps it would be wise to include some of the history of the initiation and development of this weapon which has brought it to its present stage.
First of all, I believe this missile is not the great leap forward in technology that some people would have us believe. In fact, many knowledgeable people have been concerned that while the Cruise missile and the Pershing II are meant to counter the Russian SS-20, which first came into operational service some four years ago, they are not in the minds of many its equivalent.
The second point is that the Cruise missile is not a first-strike weapon. I realize that the Leader of the New Democratic Party said that it had a potential for that. For those people whose main characteristic is a kind of paranoiac anti-Americanism, it is fashionable to claim that the Cruise missile is a quintessential first-strike weapon. Such is not the case. It is, however, a very capable second-strike weapon. The main requirement of a second-strike weapon is that it should deter a first strike. The capabilities of a first-strike weapon are that it should be able to render the enemy's nuclear armaments incapable of retaliation.
Until quite recently one seldom heard the expression "first-strike weapon" applied to any type of weapon except the intercontinental ballistic missile, the ICBM, and rightly so. To fulfil the prime requirement, the ability to destroy all of the enemy's weapons that can reach your territory, is not possible at the present time for either side, and there is very little likelihood that it will be possible within the next decade.
There are really no weapons with a first-strike capability, therefore. The main weapon that prevents the first-strike scenario from being valid is nuclear-powered, nuclear-armed submarines on both sides, cruising in the deepness of the oceans. It is not possible at the present time to track or locate them but their armament is well able to be fired with fairly good accuracy onto the enemy's homeland. So let us stop the misinformation about the Cruise missile being a great leap forward and the ultimate in first-strike weapons.
I am not alone in this, Mr. Speaker. I should like to quote someone who might be recognized by the Party on my left. Mr. Ernie Regehr is the research director for Project Ploughshares. I do not agree with Mr. Regehr very often but I respect him as one who is dedicating his life to examining the question of nuclear armaments. In a letter to The Globe and Mail on February 14 he wrote:
The term "first-strike" is used by nuclear strategists to refer to a pre-emptive nuclear attack by one side against the other's nuclear weapons system-
Any country pursuing a first-strike capability would build weapons systems that are highly accurate, with a short warning time-
Any country pursuing a first-strike capacity would be unlikely to rely on cruise missiles-
Another authority, Adam Bromke, who I believe was a former adviser to the President of the United States, said:
The cruise missile is not an offensive, "first strike" weapon. The Soviets, in fact, are more concerned about the deployment in Europe of the Pershing II-
If one compares the Cruise missile to the SS-20, the comparison is not too favourable for the Cruise. To understand this it should be pointed out that the method of propulsion and the airframe that compose the main components of the Cruise missile are very similar to the German weapon of World War II which was known as the V-l. That is, both vehicles are airbreathing, pilotless aircraft. The improvement in the Cruise missile over the V-I is mainly in the guidance system, which is much more sophisticated. The Cruise missile, however, flies along at 450 to 600 miles per hour and has a range of approximately 1,800 miles. The SS-20, which it is supposed to counter, can cover 1,800 miles in some six minutes whereas the Cruise missile would take three hours to do the same thing.
Much has been made of the fact that the Cruise missile flies close to the ground and cannot be picked up by radar. In opposition to this, one should realize that whether you can pick up the SS-20 or not makes very little difference. There is nothing in any nation's arsenal at the present time that is able to stop the SS-20 from completing its course and landing on the target. Think about that for a moment-the weapon that the Cruise missile is supposed to counter is incapable of being stopped by existing defensive weapons and can go from launch to target, 1,800 miles, in six minutes. The Cruise missile could be shot down by any modern fighter if it had sufficient warning; it can be shot down by enemy ground fire and it takes three hours to cover the same distance.
In view of time constraints, Mr. Speaker, and for other reasons I will leave the history of the Cruise missile to my distinguished colleague, the Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald), who will go into that aspect of the debate, considering that the two-track decision was taken in 1979.
A year or two after that the NATO allies announced the development of the Pershing II and the Cruise missiles must go ahead if a self-imposed deadline were to be met; that is, that deployment should start in the late fall of 1983 or in early 1984. This announcement served to bring the Russians to the negotiating table in Europe. Unfortunately, little has developed until quite recently. I for one am very encouraged by the developments of the last six months. I agree with those who say that the fact that the Russians have made concessions is not unrelated to the NATO decision to go ahead with the deployment of the Cruise and the Pershing II and to show their united determination on this matter. It is partly because of the request of the other nations in NATO that the United States has taken a conciliatory attitude as well. I feel much more optimistic than I did six months ago about the likelihood of us taking some strides towards what we all wish to do, and that is to reduce the risk of nuclear war and reduce nuclear armaments to a manageable level at least. It is to be hoped that some time in the future we will do away with them altogether.
As to the decision at the present time as to whether we should test the Cruise missile, we should bear in mind that the missile will not bear nuclear arms in Canada. We should also bear in mind that for the last 37 years we have had the benefit
June 14, 1983

of the protection of NATO and the alliance. We have not been a strong ally, while expecting to have the protection. There is a limit, 1 expect, to the extent to which our allies would be willing to accept our non-effectiveness. That might well be when we not only preach to them about nuclear weapons but would refuse to allow them to be able to test the carrying vehicles in Canadian skies. If we expect to be treated as a member of the alliance, then surely we must expect to contribute something.
I suppose the whole question comes down to whether or not nations can trust each other. There has been little in the behaviour of the U.S.S.R. in the post-World War II era to instil confidence in us that they can as a nation be trusted. I do not believe that the people of Czechoslovakia, Poland, Hungary or Afghanistan believe that Russia can or should be trusted. This presents real difficulty, of course, on the international stage. All Canadians, in fact all intelligent beings on earth, hope that nuclear arms can be first restricted, then reduced, and that greater security can be brought about by that means.
The main difference, in truth, between the peace activists and the rest of us, is how to get from the position we are in now to that future day when we hope to have the world not absolutely nuclear free, but at least have clear evidence of control. What I am saying is that our aim is identical. We wish to have that peaceful world where we can rest assured there is control over the defence forces which will lessen the likelihood of an outbreak.
The question is how we get from here to there without endangering ourselves unduly. I doubt if unilateral disarmament is the way. I doubt if sanctimonious protestations of our own purity will guarantee our safety. The recent statements made by the U.S.S.R. that they might be adopting a policy of launch and warning is what used to be called "sabre rattling".

subtopic: TESTING OF CRUISE MISSILE-HAZARDS FACED BY CIVILIAN POPULATION
TESTING OF CRUISE MISSILE-HAZARDS FACED BY CIVILIAN POPULATION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, while the Progressive Conservative Party staunchly supports Canada's commitment to NATO and, in principle, supports the testing of unarmed Cruise missiles in Canada, it is obvious that specific approvals cannot be given until full knowledge of any given test proposal is made available.
As the Member of Parliament for the region over which the testing of the Cruise missile may take place, I insist that public safety of people close to the flight path be of prime consideration, and that testing not take place until it be demonstrated that there be no danger involved for the residents in the test area.
We must be assured that the missile performs properly on short range tests in the U.S. before long range trials take place in Canada. We must be assured that the proposed flight path is nowhere near inhabited settlements.
We must know what will happen in case of a malfunction during flight, and what precautions have been taken against this possibility. Only after these and numerous other questions have been answered can we be sure that the tests can take place without danger to Canadian citizens or to their property.

NATIONAL HOCKEY LEAGUE-DENIAL OF FRANCHISE TO SASKATOON
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, yesterday, the National Hockey League took over the St. Louis Blues. NHL President, John Ziegler, said the League will "try to find suitable ownership that will take over the team and operate it in St. Louis". As you know, Saskatoon had already put in a bid, "cash on the barrell", to buy the St. Louis Blues and move the team to Saskatoon. That bid was refused by the NHL. Personally, 1 was not surprised. Professional hockey is big business, and the lords and barons of big business do not really care for little folks. Many hockey fans are from the rank and file of Mr. and Mrs. Ordinary Person.
In Saskatchewan people are born and bred hockey fans. They grow up in the "hockey player factory of the world". Saskatchewan is Gordie Howe country, Bentley country, Metz country. Mayor Cliff Wright of Saskatoon, Bill Hunter, and many others have worked hard and seriously to see that professional hockey comes to Saskatchewan. They are not going to stop now. Yesterday Mayor Wright told me that he was very pleased with the rapid progress being made in the
inquiry under the Combines Investigation Act, and the serious way in which the matter was being taken.
Other NHL teams are in trouble and will be coming up for sale. If John Ziegler feels he can stop Saskatoon by letting the League take over losing teams, he should pause to reflect.
Lastly, Saskatchewan is "next year" country. Every Saskatchewan-born person always knows that if you get "hailed out" this year, all you have to do is wait for next year.
In this vein, all seven Saskatchewan NDP federal Members are "on side" and support the efforts of Saskatoon and Mayor Wright to make Saskatchewan a National Hockey League Province.

CALL FOR MEASURES TO PROMOTE INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it was encouraging to see the reduction in our tourist deficit from $1.09 billion to $1.05 billion in the first quarter of this year compared to the same time last year.
However, the bad news is that our two main airlines are again requesting a further increase in their fares of 5 per cent, for what they claim is compensation for losses caused by the recession.
To me, and to the business community, one does not further penalize one's customers by making them pay a higher price for a product without first making every attempt to cut fat and waste from the overhead.
By raising travelling costs, by charging double the cost of a gallon of gasoline more than is paid by our neighbours to the south, by excessive taxation on spirits, and the high cost of accommodations in Canada, everything possible is being done to discourage foreign tourists from coming to Canada, and to negate real opportunity to increase tourism and to reduce our tourist deficit further.
Our country has the potential to offer tourists every type of holiday and relaxation package that is possible. All we need is for all of us and all our Governments, municipal, provincial and federal, to work together and dovetail all our efforts, and to withdraw or negate all legislation that is detrimental to tourism. As well, it is essential to give the more than 100,000 tourist operators in Canada the assistance needed to develop this very important industry to its full potential. It is my hope that all this will be noted by all Governments, and that some positive action for the Canadian tourist industry will finally be undertaken.

Madam Speaker, today I would like to put into the public record my own personal opposition and that of the New Democratic Party to the proposed testing of the Cruise missile, and take this opportunity to urge the Liberal Government to refuse the request of the United States Defence Department to test the Cruise missile in Canada.
I am not only opposed to the testing of this single weapons system, but I am also opposed to the testing or build up of all nuclear weapons and weapons systems wherever these occur or may occur. I had proposed in my private member's Bill, Bill C-678, an Act declaring Canada a nuclear weapons-free zone, that we join with others who also desire a world free of nuclear arms. At the present time there are six nations in the world which can set off a nuclear explosion, and which possess nuclear arms. It is also speculated by some that Israel, South Africa, and Pakistan also have the capability or soon will have the capability to use nuclear weapons in some cases. In addition to that, we have documented proof that there are another nine countries that could come into the nuclear weapons field within the next couple of years.

An intelligent and compassionate Canadian Government would be taking steps to halt the nuclear arms race. We are traditionally a peace loving and a peace keeping nation. We have the ability to exercise our traditions on the world stage. I believe that now is the time to do that. CALL FOR ESTABLISHMENT OF PARLIAMENTARY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, today Mitel Corporation of Kanata, in the Ottawa Valley, saw its shares drop substantially due to IBM plans to buy a 15 per cent interest in Rolm Corporation, which is Mitel's leading rival in the switching system market. Mitel lost a key contract. It shows the volatility of the new high tech market. If Mitel collapses, what will happen to its workers? An assembler, one of 152 workers laid off recently by Nabu Technology, said:
All high tech workers in the region better take notice of what's happening at NABU. We are among the lowest paid and most vulnerable industrial workers and we are all going to get the shaft.
We cannot be Luddites, that is, resisters to technological change. But neither should we be Atari Liberals, those who believe that all the answers will come from technological change.
Marshall McLuhan once said, "New means create new ends as new services create new discomforts." That is all the more reason why, in light of these recent developments, we should get going with a House of Commons committee on technological change, and learn to control high technology for the benefit of Canadian workers.
