speechtext:
Hear, hear!
June 14, 1983

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS-PROJECTION OF FUTURE JOB LOSSES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister who, as we know, has been in office for something over a decade now, a time during which the nation has been plagued with rising unemployment to the point where we now have one million more Canadians out of work than ten years ago. Most alarmingly we find that Data Resources of Canada project that this situation of having an extra one million Canadians unemployed will continue right into the 1990s. Would the Prime Minister explain to the House how we have slipped into this predicament of so many working people being without jobs? Can the Prime Minister offer any hope that the projected almost chronic unemplyment that we foresee in future years will not, in fact, materialize?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS-PROJECTION OF FUTURE JOB LOSSES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, 1 could explain. I am not sure the Hon. Member would accept or understand the explanation.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS-PROJECTION OF FUTURE JOB LOSSES
speechtext: Try me.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS-PROJECTION OF FUTURE JOB LOSSES
speechtext:
It will take a little bit of time. If the Hon. Member is patient, I will give him various reasons why this has happened. In this period of time there is a developing of new technology. There is an emerging in the Third World of countries which are getting not only into export markets that we had held in the past but are also developing higher technologies than some of the newly industrialized nations. There is a complete restructuring of the patterns of international trade. There has been a world-wide economic slow down, of which every one of the industrialized nations has been a victim. That has been caused in part by very high interest rates. That, in turn, was caused by very high inflation.
The inflationary expectations, Madam Speaker, were a result of a series of events going back to the late 1960s and the early 1970s, a time when inflation was still relatively low but when unemployment was showing signs of creeping up to 5 per cent and 6 per cent, and when the consensus, not only of the economists and specialists, but, I believe it is true to say, of most informed members of the public, was that we should try to stimulate the economy in Canada at that time to bring unemployment down from a rate which was around 6 per cent.
Unfortunately, other countries at the same time were responding to the same kind of political and social pressure. They, too, were stimulating their economies at the same time, and we laid the basis-

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS-PROJECTION OF FUTURE JOB LOSSES
speechtext: Speech.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS-PROJECTION OF FUTURE JOB LOSSES
speechtext: I have been asked for a speech. So, if the Hon. Member will be patient, l will come to the 1980s if he lets me finish with the 1970s.

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS-PROJECTION OF FUTURE JOB LOSSES
speechtext:
You will be finished in the 1980s.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS-PROJECTION OF FUTURE JOB LOSSES
speechtext: There was, therefore, a reinforcing of inflationary pressures by the economic policies of the major industrialized countries. At the same time, Madam Speaker, there was a crisis in food production.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT LEVELS-PROJECTION OF FUTURE JOB LOSSES
speechtext: Order, please. I know the question was quite general and, therefore, the answer has to be that way. But I think I have to interrupt even this answer and ask everyone to be as brief as possible. The Hon. Member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens).

Madam Speaker, my supplementary, of course, is for the Prime Minister. He has referred to changing technology during this period, and he is undoubtedly aware of a very recent report from the Conference Board in Canada. It points out that one of the disappointing aspects of the Canadian economic performance over the past decade has been the sharp deterioration in productivity growth.
As the Prime Minister undoubtedly knows, since 1977, while our productivity growth was flat, in Japan it went up 29 per cent, and in England it went up 13 per cent.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.
My question to the Prime Minister-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I will stop it right now because the whole Question Period will go that way. The Hon. Member's question should be brief, as should the answers.
If technology has been the problem leading to our unemployment, why is Canada's record the worst of major industrial nations, for productivity growth?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is just making up that statistic. It is not the worst. Some countries have been successful in productivity. The Hon. Member mentioned Japan, but most of the other industrialized countries, including the United States, have suffered very low rates of productivity, presumably because in the previous part of the economic cycle productivity had been very high in Canada and in the Unites States.
What happened in the 1970s was that Canada had the fastest rate of job creation of any industrialized nation. We were dedicated then to the creation of jobs. I repeat that we had the fastest growing labour force of any of the major industrialized nations and that we had a record much higher than even Japan or the United States in job creation. We tackled that problem.
In so far as technology is concerned, the Hon. Member has heard the budget speech. He has heard the Minister of Finance indicate the funds which would be going into research and development. He has heard the Minister of Finance announce

June 14, 1983
Oral Questions
the creation of a centre for productivity. We are asking for the co-operation at this time of the various decision makers in society to help us with that centre. I am talking of the labour side and of the managerial side.

Madam Speaker, again my question is directed to the Prime Minister who, undoubtedly, is taking some comfort today in the plight of other countries. If he wants to compare Canada, perhaps he would compare its record with that of the United States since 1975, where we find that our real growth has been less, our employment creation has been less, and our unemployment has risen faster. Why are the Americans more successful in coping with current economic conditions in the world than his Government in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not know to what period the Hon. Member is referring. If we take the whole period of the 1970s, or indeed the whole period since 1968, which is the date that sticks in the Hon. Member's craw, we have created jobs at a faster rate than the United States and, indeed, than even Japan. We had to be attacking the problem of unemployment here-of employment, rather-because we had the fastest growing labour force. There were other countries like Germany and Switzerland which could export their unemployment by sending their gastarbeiten home. We did not use that approach in Canada. We created jobs.
So far as the ranking of Canada is concerned, the Minister of Finance just handed me an analysis in The Gazette this morning which indicates that Canada has gone up in the past year from twelfth to sixth. Even if the Hon. Member is only looking at the past year, he has the answer. If he wants to look at the whole period of the decade, I repeat that in terms of job creation, in terms of unemployment fighting, in terms of bringing down inflation, and in terms of exports, we rank among the two or three best. In some instances we are the best, such as job creation. In others, such as inflation, some other countries did better than we did. But on the average we did very well, and the Hon. Member should not try to hide that.

subsubtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLERS' DISPUTE-PROGRESS OF MEDIATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Labour regarding the grain handling situation on the West Coast. I know the Minister appointed Mr. Kelly on Friday as labour mediator. He is a well respected person in that field. Also we know that the parties met yesterday and again this morning at 9.30 Vancouver time. Could the Minister bring us up to date on how the negotiations are progressing?

subsubtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLERS' DISPUTE-PROGRESS OF MEDIATION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member has correctly stated the situation. Meetings are taking place. It would be inappropriate for me to make any further comments, except to say that we have a highly respected official representing Labour Canada involved, and that we hope the outcome will be a positive one.
speakername: Hon.   Chas. L. Caccia@Minister of Labour

subsubtopic: WEST COAST GRAIN HANDLERS' DISPUTE-PROGRESS OF MEDIATION
speechtext: I appreciate the Minister's response.

Madam Speaker, I would just like to point out to the Minister that this is a very crucial industry not only to western Canada but to the country as a whole, and that it would be very unfortunate if there were any kind of work stoppage in this vital industry. Again I ask him to ensure that his Department stays involved to see that everything is done and that there is a settlement without a work stoppage.
Madam Speaker, the presence of the senior assistant deputy minister in charge of mediation is proof of the importance the Government attributes to this particular situation.
speakername: Hon.   Chas. L. Caccia@Minister of Labour

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR NEGOTIATION OF TEST BAN TREATY ON AIR LAUNCHED MISSILES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister concerning nuclear disarmament. He knows that the two series of talks taking place in Geneva on nuclear disarmament do not have any relevance whatsoever to the testing of air launched Cruise missiles either by the Soviet Union or by the United States. To be specific, even if an agreement is reached in those talks at Geneva, for which we all hope, it would still permit either the United States or the Soviet Union to test an air launched Cruise.
Given the qualitative horrific nature of that particular weapon, and the possibility of both the United States and the Soviet Union proceeding each in its own way to test it, will the Prime Minister take an important step for peace and propose to each country that they begin negotiations, with the view of obtaining agreement on a test ban treaty on air launched Cruise missiles?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR NEGOTIATION OF TEST BAN TREATY ON AIR LAUNCHED MISSILES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as far as test ban treaties are concerned, certainly I can indicate that Canada will continue advocating them and, indeed, trying to enjoin the major nuclear powers to accept a general test ban treaty, not only a partial one. The Hon. Member is correct in stating that Cruises are not directly involved in the negotiations in Geneva. Perhaps is talking in the sense that they were not excluded in SALT II, that neither side found it advantageous to say that they would not be developing the Cruise. Of course he is not correct if he is
June 14, 1983

implying-and 1 do not think he is-that the INF negotiations going on at this time are not concerned with the Cruise. They are. For instance, we know that during the walk in the woods between the two main negotiators there was a recognition by both sides that there would be some Cruise deployed.
1 am in sympathy with the hopes of the Hon. Member that there would be a total test ban, but I have to point out to him that it is well known at this time that the Soviets are testing Cruise missiles. They have an advance over us on the short range missiles; they are testing long range missiles. Secretary Andropov said so publicly last December. Therefore the case we have to solve is whether we should unilaterally stop testing when we know this and the other side says that it is testing.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER INITIATE NEGOTIATIONS
REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER INITIATE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the precise point at issue is to present a concrete challenge, both to the Soviet Union and to the United States, on their willingness with reference to this very specific weapon, to enter into a test ban agreement. I suspect that in his conversations with Mr. Gorbachev, when he was in this country, the Prime Minister might have had with him on this matter and might have obtained some indication that the Soviet Union might be interested in that. I do not know. It will be interesting to see what the Prime Minister says.
I repeat the question. In the interests of mankind in not having either country proceed with the development of this missile beyond the level of development that has already taken place, will he go out front and publicly urge both the United States and the Soviet Union to negotiate toward a test ban treaty concerning air launched Cruise missiles?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER INITIATE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, that, of course, is exactly what I urged when I proposed in 1978, and again in 1980, the strategy of suffocation. By another name, that is stopping of all testing of new weapons and new weapons delivery systems whether they be in the laboratory or on the ground. That is what I proposed to both sides. As I have reported repeatedly to the House, neither the Americans nor the Soviets, nor for that matter the French nor the British, have been prepared to say that they would no longer test weapons. There is a partial test ban treaty but it does not cover delivery systems. It does not cover developing new weapons. It does not even cover testing those weapons by underground explosion.
Once again, I can only say that certainly this side of the House is very anxious to see that kind of a treaty be developed. I did not talk directly with Mr. Gorbachev on that particular subject. I did talk a great deal about the SS-20s and asked why they were deployed. I had occasion to report on that to the House previously.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER INITIATE NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister knows that the proposal he made at the United Nations, with which
Oral Questions
we are in sympathy and which he acknowledged obtained agreement from neither side, goes well beyond the very specific kind of test ban treaty I am talking about, which refers exclusively to the air launched Cruise missile.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT FREE VOTE BE HELD ON CRUISE TESTING ISSUE
REQUEST THAT FREE VOTE BE HELD ON CRUISE TESTING ISSUE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I have a final question concerning a point raised by one of the Prime Minister's own Members earlier today on the importance of this issue to Canada. Will the Prime Minister take steps to ensure that his House Leader will view the vote that will take place later today on the important matter of testing the Cruise in Canada as not being a vote of confidence, and therefore allow his Members to vote as their consciences dictate? I assure the Prime Minister that is the way we would view this matter on this side of the House.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST THAT FREE VOTE BE HELD ON CRUISE TESTING ISSUE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I am afraid I cannot answer that particular suggestion with as much understanding and sympathy as I tried to understand the two previous ones. The NDP is playing games, just as the Tories played games when they had a non-confidence motion on property rights. We are voting the last supply day today. The fate of the Government hangs on whether we get supply or not. If the Hon. Member is suggesting that we change the rules and we get unanimous consent that this not be a supply vote or a confidence vote, and if they now report to me that there has been agreement, I will consult with a few Ministers and give an answer. As far as I know, the question is hypothetical. If we are going to change the rules and say that a non-confidence motion is not a non-confidence motion, then I hope we will do that on many occasions other than just this one.

subtopic: DENIAL OF NATIONAL HOCKEY LEAGUE FRANCHISE TO SASKATOON-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER INTERVENE
DENIAL OF NATIONAL HOCKEY LEAGUE FRANCHISE TO SASKATOON-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER INTERVENE
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. The National Hockey League is resorting to extraordinary efforts to keep the St. Louis Blues franchise from coming to Saskatchewan. It includes the disbanding of the team and the dispersal of its players. I know that the Government has been helpful in terms of the Combines Investigation Act. 1 appreciate that very much, as do many Canadians. I would like to ask the Prime Minister whether, on behalf of the Government and the people of Canada, he would be prepared to communicate with the President of the Board of Governors of the National Hockey League, Mr. John Ziegler, indicating support for the application by Saskatchewan for the transfer of the National Hockey League team to that Province.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: DENIAL OF NATIONAL HOCKEY LEAGUE FRANCHISE TO SASKATOON-REQUEST THAT PRIME MINISTER INTERVENE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have been discussing this very matter with some of

June 14, 1983
Oral Questions
my advisers, including the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and the Minister responsible for sport. I have had the advice of one of our good Saskatchewan Liberals, Mr. Doug Richardson. I am happy that there is also one elected Tory who is interested in this matter. I will report to him later today or this week as to whether there is some way in which 1 can use my good offices to influence the President of the National Hockey League.

Madam Speaker, I can only thank the Prime Minister for his consideration of this important matter which has the support of so many Canadians and which, in my opinion, is an important ingredient in terms of national unity. Indeed, I understand that the Members of the New Democratic Party are changing their position and may in fact support this application. In view of the fact that Saskatchewan has contributed so much to the National Hockey League, and that indeed the people of Canada in various ways support the National Hockey League, such as through the use of the air waves and the amateur draft, supported by taxpayers' money, is it not a reasonable expectation for the people of Saskatchewan to get a fair hearing from the NHL for a legitimate application for a franchise within their Province?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the Hon. Member is making a representation. I have indicated to him that I have had such representations from people on this side. I hope they will be made known to the President of the National Hockey League and the members of the board.

subsubtopic: TASK FORCE RECOMMENDATIONS-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. The much heralded task force report on the auto industry was presented to the Minister nearly a month ago, yet the Government continues to keep this vital sector in the dark, denying the opportunity for long-range planning in that industry and thereby creating the potential for massive employment. Can the Minister tell us at least whether he supports the thrust of the report, if not the details of it? If so, what is he going to do about it? If he has not made up his mind about the report, when, for goodness sake, is he going to come up with a decision so the industry will know where it is heading?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subsubtopic: TASK FORCE RECOMMENDATIONS-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I indicated the day after the report was made public, the Government will be giving serious consideration to the recommendations of the report, particularly
because of the dedicated work the members of the task force put into it. We will discuss the report over the course of the summer and respond some time in the fall.

subsubtopic: TASK FORCE RECOMMENDATIONS-MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the industry wants to know how long the Government will take to come up with a decision. That is the question I put to the Minister.

subtopic: VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS ON JAPANESE IMPORTS-EXPIRY OF AGREEMENT
VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS ON JAPANESE IMPORTS-EXPIRY OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of State for International Trade I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. With respect to the voluntary restraints on Japanese auto imports which expire at the end of this month, the travelling but ineffective Minister of State for International Trade said in this House last week that a decision will be made soon on that and, if not, he would "recommend other appropriate steps to the Government". Can the Minister tell this House and the industry whether an agreement in fact will be forthcoming before the end of this month when it expires and, if not, what those other so-called "appropriate steps" will be that the Minister of State for International Trade was talking about?

speakeroldname: Hon. Ed Lumley (Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce; Minister of Regional Economic Expansion
subtopic: VOLUNTARY RESTRAINTS ON JAPANESE IMPORTS-EXPIRY OF AGREEMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, with respect to the first part of the Hon. Member's question, if he checks he will find that the cochairmen of the task force indicated that they did not expect to get an answer on the major thrust of the task force recommendations until the Fall. Our thinking is along the same line. Regarding the Member's second question, I do not profess to speak for any of my colleagues. When the Minister of State for International Trade returns, I am sure he can answer the Hon. Member more directly than I can.

subsubtopic: TESTING OF CRUISE MISSILE-TIMING OF GOVERNMENT DECISION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister regarding Cruise missile testing. The Prime Minister has said on many occasions, most recently on March 24, and I quote:
-our judgment of how the other track was proceeding-
That is negotiations.
-would influence us in deciding whether we would go with the Cruise or not.
On June 1 the Prime Minister said that he would hope to be hearing "very specific proposals rejected or accepted before the end of December", in Geneva. May I ask the Prime
June 14, 1983

Minister if this therefore means that there would be no question of accepting the request for testing the air launched Cruise missile before December?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: TESTING OF CRUISE MISSILE-TIMING OF GOVERNMENT DECISION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when 1 made that statement I did not know when the request would be made of us. It was made of us yesterday. I answered a question in the House yesterday indicating that we would be examining this question, that the Minister of National Defence would be bringing his appreciation of the situation to his colleagues, and that we would be making a decision. I do not know when we will be making that decision, Madam Speaker.
1 do know that there has been some indication of flexibility by both sides in recent months. Secretary Andropov moved some distance in December and then he moved again in March, I believe it was, when he offered to count warheads rather than delivery missiles. President Reagan has made other moves as regards the hotline, and has made other suggestions as regards confidence building measures, but also very recently he has made an offer to count warheads rather than missiles, and he has not held to the figure of 800 and some, which he wanted the START talks to bring the Soviets down to. He has recognized that the Soviets wanted more than that number.
There has been some show of flexibility on both sides. I can only say that the Government will continue to pursue its duties as it sees them under the two-track system, and we will continue monitoring the situation. The Cruise, in terms of the request itself, will only be tested next year, but it is logical that Canada continue to act as though it had confidence and faith in its main ally.

Madam Speaker, the Prime Minister said that the Cruise would only be tested next year. May I remind him that he said quite explicitly that the negotiations would influence us in deciding whether we would test the Cruise or not. From what he has said, negotiations are proceeding, both sides showing some flexibility. I therefore repeat my question. Will he allow a really adequate length of time for negotiations to continue, both IMF and START, as the air launched Cruise has more to do with START, before there is any thought whatsoever given to testing the Cruise?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext:
Indeed, Madam Speaker, I have said that negotiations will influence us, and that is why I have given examples of the negotiations which have influenced us. I must say that I feel more secure with the possibility of successful negotiations now than I felt several months ago before Andropov and Reagan made their offers. So, Madam Speaker, that is the only answer I can give. We have to make our decision on the basis of the facts as we know them and as we see them.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: CRITERIA GOVERNING EXPENDITURE OF MONEY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and deals with the approval that Cabinet gave to an expenditure of $345 million known as the Indian economic development fund. I would ask the Minister whether this money is to be spent in accordance with the Cabinet memorandum of April 29, namely, that the money is not to be spent in accordance with need or with any social objectives such as housing but rather in accordance with criteria designed to promote urban entrepreneurship and to promote the rewarding of Indian entrepreneurs who are Liberal supporters.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: CRITERIA GOVERNING EXPENDITURE OF MONEY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, it is not an Indian economic development fund, it is a Native Economic Development Fund. It includes Metis and other natives. As well, Madam Speaker, my colleague, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, has responsibility for the corporation. I believe that the Hon. Member should direct his comments to that Minister.

Madam Speaker, if the Minister thinks that the people for whom he has a very special trust responsibility are not natives, then I would like him to explain his portfolio. He has a very special trust responsibility and I wonder how he can exercise that trust responsibility, a component of which is economic stability in native communities, when he gives away $345 million to a colleague of his who manages small businesses.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I did not say that Indians were not Natives. I did say that the title of the fund is the Native Economic Development Fund, and that includes Metis and Indians. If the Hon. Member will direct his question to my colleague, the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism, who has already consulted with Mr. Ahenakew, head of the AFM, about his participation in it, I am sure that the Hon. Member will find that there is no doubt that they will receive moneys in addition to the Indian economic development moneys that are already in the Department that we disburse each year for Indian economic development. Therefore, Indians will have two pools of funds from which to draw in order to get ahead with native economic development.

subsubtopic: FREEZING OF BAND TRUST ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Indian Affairs

June 14, 1983
Oral Questions
and Northern Development. Bankruptcies will force band councils to close down their administration offices very soon if the Minister continues to freeze their trust accounts as he refuses to negotiate with them a mutually acceptable accounting practice. Does the Minister recognize the administrative difficulties caused by and the paternalistic effect of withholding Indian bands' own trust accounts unless they submit to his financial circulars?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: FREEZING OF BAND TRUST ACCOUNTS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have found, and again this may be an example of it, that when Indian financial matters are such that they might result in some non-Indians in a community not getting paid, then the Hon. Members opposite are all too ready for me to become paternalistic and interfere in Indian affairs. I would like all Hon. Members to remember what the Official Opposition are now saying. They do not want a Minister who is paternalistic and who will interfere in financial handlings, and I wish that in asking future questions they would be consistent throughout the remainder of this Parliament at least.
It is very refreshing for me to hear that the Hon. Member does not want this Minister to interfere in the financial affairs of the bands. 1 can only tell him that any interference in the affairs of the particular band in question, Madam Speaker, has happened simply because the affairs have been found to be irregular, and not because we wish to be paternalistic. Under the Financial Administration act, certain actions are required on the part of our Department. Until Parliament wishes to change those regulations, we are bound by Parliament to carry them out.

Madam Speaker, the Minister professes to be doing everything possible to transfer decision-making authority to Indian bands, yet in the case of the Stony Indian band, where Indian mineral contracts were renegotiated without the band's knowledge or participation, his actions were inconsistent with what he just told me. I wonder whether he is continuing this practice or whether he will in fact live up to his promise to turn decision-making authority and responsibility over to Indians when those decisions affect them directly.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I wish that the Hon. Member would talk to his colleagues who have been asking me questions about West Bank for the last year. Some of his colleagues have feelings that are very close to his feelings about how I should be interfering in the affairs of that particular Indian band. But let me tell the Hon. Member again that it is only with reluctance that we do interfere, and in this particular case it was not done with any great enthusiasm and was
done only because we were legally required to do so in order to live up to the obligations we have to Parliament under the appropriate legislation.
I will check into the situation again in order to report back to the Hon. Member. If there is any way around this provision that will not infringe upon the freedom of action of the Indian people, I am quite prepared to undertake it, but I do not see a way around it at the moment.

subsubtopic: REPORTED SURVEILLANCE OF GROUPS OPPOSED TO CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General. Recently I received reliable information to the effect that the RCMP are involved in surveillance of groups and individuals organizing protests against the testing of the Cruise missile in Canada, that a well respected national peace and development organization is also the object of surveillance, and that the antiCruise demonstration planned for Cold Lake, Alberta, on June 26 is the object of a special task force of the Security Service. Is the Minister aware of these activities on the part of the RCMP? If so, can he explain the reasons for them and, if not, would he inquire into the matter?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
subsubtopic: REPORTED SURVEILLANCE OF GROUPS OPPOSED TO CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I should like the opportunity to inquire into the matter and I would appreciate having any additional information that the Hon. Member has.

subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING SURVEILLANCE OF OTHER GROUPS
INQUIRY RESPECTING SURVEILLANCE OF OTHER GROUPS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, if the Minister makes inquiries and finds that the facts are as I have indicated, will he inquire if the Security Service is going to put Members of Parliament under surveillance, or leaders of church communities who have expressed opposition to the testing of the Cruise missile?

speakeroldname: Hon. Bob Kaplan (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: INQUIRY RESPECTING SURVEILLANCE OF OTHER GROUPS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I can certainly assure the Hon. Member that the peace movement is not and could not be a target of surveillance within the meaning of the mandate of the Security Service. However, any individuals who by virtue of their activities or goals and objectives, are targets within the meaning of the mandate of the Security Service, would be the object of surveillance whether they were infiltrating the peace movement or any other non-targeted activity or movement within the country.
June 14, 1983

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA ISSUANCE OF DISMISSAL NOTICES TO EMPLOYEES
PETRO-CANADA ISSUANCE OF DISMISSAL NOTICES TO EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Within the last few days well over 1,000 employees of Petro-Canada were given termination notices. A PetroCan spokesman said that this was necessary because there is an overlapping of staff in the wake of acquisitions such as Petrofina and BP Canada. In essence, in the height of a recession, the Government taxes Canadians, the money is used to build Petro-Canada's empire, and thousands of Canadians are put out of work.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in addressing the House just before one o'clock, I was taking particular issue with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne) and the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) for looking at nuclear war in a very conventional sense rather than realizing it is not only quantitatively but totally different from conventional war, such as World War I and World War II. It is because a nuclear exchange could result, indeed it is 99 per cent likely that it would result, in a nuclear holocaust that so many people in the world today are becoming concerned with the enormous nuclear arsenals. I would remind Hon. Members that it was the equivalent of 15,000 tons of tnt which exploded over and devastated Hiroshima. Today the world's nuclear arsenals are the equivalent of 16 billion tons of tnt, which could destroy the world many times over along with all life on it.
It also seems to me that the Minister is out of date when he talks about the doctrine of deterrence. I think most people saw that as the deterrence of war. Nowadays the military and civilian strategists are not talking about deterring nuclear war; they are talking about fighting and winning a nuclear war. This, too, has been so alarming to the public everywhere. It is bad enough to have a strategy of nuclear deterrence, but it is far, far worse to have a doctrine of fighting and prevailing in a nuclear war. The Minister has absolutely no concept of this radical change in thinking about nuclear arms. He stills talks about the doctrine of deterrence as it was talked about almost a generation ago, not recognizing that we have gone far beyond the real needs of deterrence.

June 14, 1983
Supply
It is significant that the Cruise missile is not simply a weapon of deterrence. It is designed for the purpose of intimidation and to fight a nuclear war. Whether we talk about the land, air or submarine-launched Cruise missile, the whole point is its pinpoint accuracy so that it can be used to take out missiles in their silos. In other words, it is designed for fighting a nuclear war, not deterring a nuclear war. Again, the Minister and others seem to have simply not recognized what has been taking place in the nuclear war strategy with the development of a new generation of nuclear weapons like the Cruise missile.
A third area where the Government and the Minister are so old fashioned and out of date is that of Canada playing a nonnuclear role in the alliance. There was a time when Canada was moving in that direction. Indeed, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took credit for it in answer to a question on April 22, 1983 when he said:
-I have done a great deal in Canada to denuclearize our whole approach to defence. I did that in Canada and I did that in NATO by denuclearizing our planes in Germany.
What we are asking for in this motion today is a logical extension of those independent initiatives we took by saying not only will we not deploy nuclear weapons on our soil, not only will we not have our forces in Europe nuclearized, but we will also refrain from testing any nuclear weapon delivery systems. It seems to me that is part of the logic of denuclearization.
For some reason the Government has now decided not to continue a non-nuclear role. Our military and political commitment in Europe, indeed with the United States, does not need to be expressed in nuclear terms. I have heard many Members on the Government side and within the Conservative Party say that, so why, then, are so many of those same Members urging us to play once again a nuclear capable role, which is exactly what testing is all about? Elave we simply lost all capacity for taking independent initiatives, for doing an independent assessment, or for a less uncritical acceptance of the nuclear armed strategy we hear about from Washington and elsewhere? Why do we simply and uncritically accept that if they want us to test the Cruise we will test the Cruise? It really has nothing to do with NATO, or NORAD commitments, or anything else. What it has to do with, I am sorry to say, is that we have become more and more integrated into the economic and military doctrines and values of Washington. We have therefore simply abandoned any independent judgment, any independent evaluation, any independent decisionmaking with regard to alliance nuclear weapons policies.
That is also what the Canadian public is so alarmed about. The public would like to see their Government taking a lead among the smaller nations of the world, among members of the alliance, like the lead taken by Norway, which is still a faithful member of the alliance, in saying no to any further escalation of the nuclear arms race. What the Canadian public wants is a freeze, bilateral, mutual, verifiable, followed by
massive reductions; to use George Kennan's phrase, "massive reductions and final elimination". We are not discussing any old weapon. We are discussing nuclear weapons which could see the end of this planet, whether accidentally or deliberately, and it is more likely to be accidental.
This is what the public is crying for from its Government. It thought the Government might do this a few years ago, referring to the policies of the Prime Minister, both of Canadian initiatives in denuclearization and promoting the concept of a strategy of suffocation by all the powers. Now it does not see either of them being followed by the Government.
We could untie ourselves without hurt or harm to our economy or to our relationship with the United States. We could untie ourselves from this total dependence, this uncritical acceptance of everything that is done. We could join other smaller nations and medium-sized nations in the alliance and in relations with other nations and members of other alliances in developing nuclear weapons free zones. Once one develops a nuclear weapons free zone, whether it is a single country or a group of countries, one is saying; "We will not be subject to nuclear intimidation", and that is one of the most significant aspects of the development of nuclear weapons free zones. We would be free to pursue the goals that everyone in the world wants to reach, namely, the goal of peace, freedom and security.
I close by emphasizing again, as strongly as possible, that the escalation of nuclear arms holdings does not provide security, either national security or international security, let alone personal security. We must realize, not that we must drop the word "security" but that the way to attain security, mutual security, national and international, is ultimately by ending the nuclear arms race. Only when we have done that and, as Canadians, have participated in reaching that end will everyone feel secure once again.

On the other hand, the issue of missiles prompted acrimonious debate between the parties in that election held just recently. The tenor of the exchanges was harsher than in any post-war election. Some analysts have concluded that the strong emotions and fears raised may very well leave lasting scars on the population.
The divergent attitudes of political parties in West Germany toward the INF deployment provoked an unprecedent degree of outside involvement in that general election. The Soviet Union was notable for opposing deployment and intimidating those who favoured it. They used the carrot and stick approach as they frequently do. Soviet Foreign Minister Andrei Gromyko visited the FRG in January and figured prominently in the partisan domestic campaign. Painting a picture of the U.S.S.R. as benevolent and committed to a reasonable arms agreement in the Geneva INF talks, he characterized the Reagan administration as "gamblers and con men", insensitive to European problems and uncommitted to a successful outcome at Geneva.
We all know President Reagan's conclusion. He said this:
These actions reflect a bipartisan consensus on arms control, and new flexibility in the negotiations-steps to be viewed seriously by the Soviets and all others who have a stake in world peace. To the leaders of the Soviet Union, I urge that this new opportunity not be lost. To America's friends and allies around the world, I say that your steadfast support for the goals of both deterrence and arms control is essential in the future. To Congress and to the American people, 1 say let us continue to work together in a bipartisan spirit so that these days will be spoken of in the future as the time when America turned a corner. Let us put our differences behind us. Let us demonstrate measured flexibility in our approach, while remaining strong in our determination to reach our objectives of arms reductions, stability, and security. Let us be leaders in the cause of peace.
That is what we should be, Mr. Speaker. It is what Mr, Kohl in West Germany wants. It is what Prime Minister Thatcher wants, and she has just come through a very successful election. It is what the leaders in Holland want. Italy is going into an election, and that is what its leaders want. It is what the socialist movement in Italy wants; it is what members of the Communist Party in Italy want. They want a negotiated peace. It is what Canadians want. We differ on how we reach those goals, but at least let us support the leaders of the alliance who are our friends. Let us not go off on tangents and confuse an unsophisticated Canadian public on the nuclear debate. We must not do that either wittingly or unwittingly, and that is why I chose to take some time to speak about this. 1 am amazed that it was necessary to do so as I thought everyone understood the difference, the role and purpose of an air-launched Cruise missile compared to that of a ground-launched, Cruise missile or a sea-launched Cruise missile. Entirely different technologies are involved and each has a different purpose and a different role.
West Germany continues to support the principles of the December, 1979, decision. It was not easy for the leader. I tell this the way I understand it, Mr. Speaker. Mr. Kohl's victory did not necessarily come out of the debate, nor did the opposition to it. The growth of the Green Party in West Germany has been noted but it has lost most of its credibility.
In the United Kingdom, Prime Minister Thatcher did not waver at all. She has supported the 1979 agreement since its beginning. What nappened to the coalition in that country? We all saw the manifesto printed down one side of the page
Supply
and another manifesto down the other. There were 21 points, 17 of them identical. If Hon. Members would do a little research, they would understand why honourable men and women of good will always defer to the right pursuit of peace. They do not necessarily reject other courses toward peace but they will always accept the right course.
How many Governments are there in Europe? We have 15 allies in NATO. Are we always right? Are we the only ones who know what is right? In Canada we have little choice but to support the knowledgeable decisions of the Government, and I hope this is a position that this Party would take. We have the same qualifications as the Government with respect to any escalation of the nuclear arms race. Those things are clear and are well set out. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Victoria, has done that, and others will follow.
Prime Minister Thatcher's Government repeatedly rejected the Soviet demand that the United Kingdom's independent nuclear forces be included in the Geneva INF negotiations. The Government has taken the position, shared by the NATO allies, that the Soviet posture is, in fact, an attempt to decouple the U.S. from Europe by excluding U.S. nuclear weapons systems from Europe. United Kingdom officials have argued that the British and French independent nuclear systems should not be included for several reasons; they are by definition and nature strategic and not theatre forces; they are minimal deterrent forces vis-a-vis the vast Soviet nuclear arsenal, and the INF negotiations are strictly bilateral. The March, 1982, U.K. white paper did indicate, however, that if circumstances were to change significantly, that is, if Soviet military capabilities and the threat they posed to the United Kingdom were to be reduced substantially, the U.K. would, of course, be prepared to review its position in relation to arms control. They have said these things. They are in place. They are part of the debate. It is incumbent upon us to be aware of it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to open my remarks by commenting on the role of the Department of National Defence. The role is a very specific one. It is the protection of this bountiful land of ours against aggression and the preservation of peace and freedom. It must do this in the real world where there are foreign powers who do not share our values of freedom and dignity for each human being. Peace has different meanings and perceptions in different lands. For example, the Soviet Union's definition, as expressed by Lenin many years ago, was that peace simply means communist world control.
In this world, nuclear weapons do exist. We cannot wish them away or demonstrate them away. They will not go away. They exist as weapons in the hands of sovereign states, friend or foe alike, such as the Soviet Union, the People's Republic of China, the United Kingdom, and most likely other countries as well. Indeed, these terrible weapons are in the hands of nations whose leadership is dedicated to the very antithesis of democracy and freedom. One such superpower is the Soviet Union.
A nuclear weapon is not just a qualitative advance over previous weapons. They have added a new dimension, not only to warfare but to our very human existence. There can be no winners in a nuclear war, but nuclear arms are a reality that we must face as a nation and address as a Defence Department.
In light of its size and geography, its vast and unpopulated frontiers, its three ocean coastlines and its wide expanse of ice and snow in the north, Canada relies heavily on its alliance with the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and operates under an allied defence system. There is no doubt but that Canada's security depends on co-operation with our neighbour to the south as well as with our other partners in NATO. The
Supply
motion today deals with our participation in NATO concerning deterrence, which is interpreted as an escalation in nuclear arms.
In the first place, the House is asked to oppose escalation of the nuclear arms race by any nation. Inherent in this proposition are two implications: the first is that there is in progress a "nuclear arms race". The second is that the pace of this arms race is quickening in that its dimensions are getting larger; that it is indeed escalating.
Historically the concept of an arms race has been applied to a situation in which potential military rivals or adversaries have engaged in competitive programs of armament or rearmament, each with the objective of gaining superiority over the other. Is this in fact the process in which, with respect to their nuclear arsenals, the two superpowers and, more generally, NATO and the Warsaw Pact are now engaged? If so, Mr. Speaker, if we conclude that the two rival superpowers on the one hand and NATO and the Warsaw Pact on the other hand are indeed engaged in a race for superiority in nuclear weapons, do we not then have to examine how that race was started and what are its current dynamics before we can reach sensible conclusions as to how it can best be halted and as to the effects upon the arms race of particular weapon decisions taken by either? As the Minister said in his statement on Estimates to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence on March 15:
For two decades the Soviet Union has had the potential to threaten Western Europe with intermediate-range ballistic missiles armed with nuclear weapons, without there ever having been a large number of similar systems available in the allied military structure of NATO Europe. NATO was able to tolerate this situation as long as the United States enjoyed a superiority in intercontinental ballistic missiles which kept not only the Soviet Union's counterparts, but also its land-based Intermediate-Range Nuclear Force (INF) missiles facing Europe in rough balance. Since the Soviet Union has become equally strong in intercontinental weapons, and since this rough strategic parity has been codified by the SALT agreements, there is now a greater need to correct the pronounced imbalance in intermediate-range weapons, either through a reduction by the Soviet Union or by the installation of some offsetting system by the West. In the area of intermediate-range weapons, the Soviet Union made a great and deliberate leap forward with the introduction of SS-20 missiles. The North Atlantic Alliance members were understandably concerned by this new threat to the territory of its European states.
When early efforts to dissuade the Soviet Union from deploying its SS-20s failed, Western governments took the 'two-track' decision in December 1979 to modernize NATO's intermediate-range weapons through the introduction of the Pershing II and Ground Launched Cruise Missile (GLCM) and to offer arms control negotiations to the Soviet Union, an unprecedented procedure in which negotiations were proposed on new weapons systems before their deployment and whose objective it is to bring about a limitation of these systems in both East and West at the lowest possible level, desirably zero. Canada is convinced, as are her European allies, that the threat posed by the presence of the Soviet Union's long-range land-based INF missiles cannot be ignored. Though we greatly prefer to deal with this threat through negotiations, we also recognize and support the requirement for NATO to negotiate from a position of strength."
The lesson of history is that peace is made more likely by a balance of power; so long as East and West maintain broadly equivalent forces, there is little danger of war. But the West can only sustain its part of this relationship if its own forces are kept up to date. There is also a need to guard against

June 14, 1983
Supply
attempts by the Soviet Union to achieve military superiority in any particular area, such as the INF. Moreover, such decisions are taken only after the most careful consideration. They are not autonomous or planned. Arms control aims to control this competition, to stabilize the balance and, if possible, to reduce the level of forces on both sides.
Among the Hon. Members opposite who put forward the resolution before us, there is a number who have philosophical leanings. I would suggest that even the best philosophers would benefit from minimal knowledge of history. It would not have taken much research to show that the West simply cannot be charged with escalating the nuclear arms race. One does not even require this degree of historical expertise to observe that the only conceivable cause for war between East and West would be a Soviet military attack.
Cruise missiles are not a new weapon, nor will they give a new twist to the arms race. The Soviet Union is deploying its new SS-20s now, and has been doing so since 1977. One new SS-20 missile has been deployed on an average each week, to a total of 350, each with three warheads.
From their silence over the past six years, one can only conclude that those who tabled the resolution today were not troubled by such developments. The NATO Cruise missiles, on the other hand, which are the object of the resolution, are not due to start arriving in Europe until the end of this year at the earliest, and only then if a satisfactory arms control agreement is not reached.
In taking its modernization decision, NATO agreed that before the first missile arrived, a major effort should be made to prevent an arms spiral. As evidence of this, the Americans have already withdrawn 1,000 nuclear warheads from Europe, and they will remove one more for every new warhead deployed.
It is worth recalling that at the start the Russians refused to even talk. It was only when faced with NATO's determination to proceed with the modernization decision that the Russians concluded that they could not get what they wanted on a onesided basis and agreed to negotiate.
The resolution must be opposed. It is flawed in its essence. It has no redeeming features. It does not even call for a lessening of reliance on nuclear weapons through improvements to our conventional defences. Rather, it betrays a state of mind prepared to acquiesce in Soviet strategic superiority and to dismantle or disavow any weapons systems on our soil that the Soviet Union might regard as being provocative. The resolution bears eloquent if unwitting witness to the policital dividends that the development of nuclear superiority brings in its wake.
In conclusion, let me say that living with nuclear weapons is one of the inevitable results of mankind's unrelenting search for knowledge, just as are the many benefits that we enjoy in medicine, communications and agriculture. Nuclear weapons cannot be disinvented. We must learn to live with them. We need to create an environment where there is stability between
nuclear equipped forces so that there be no incentive to attempt aggression.
Nuclear deterrence is a dreadful form of security, but it is effective, it has proven itself, and it does prevent the horrors of any type of war. However, to be effective, it must be such that there is no doubt but that initiating a nuclear engagement would entail absolutely unacceptable costs and punishment to the initiator. I will therefore vote against the resolution.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are today debating an issue of the utmost gravity to mankind. In doing so, surely we can agree that no one individual in this House and no single Party has a monopoly on the desire for peace in this world. Surely that is a goal we all seek. Yet I find the wording of this NDP motion before us today demeans and belittles the seriousness of this critical debate.
In the confusion and controversy that presently surrounds the role that Canada may be called upon to play in the testing of the Cruise missile guidance system, we should begin by recognizing that a limited nuclear war in Europe would be disastrous. Not only would it devastate the towns and cities of that continent but it is inconceivable that it would remain limited in terms of the size of the weapons used or of the geographic area. There are no obvious fire breaks that would halt it. There are no sure ways of limiting the use of these weapons to the so-called "little ones". To use the word "limited" is to commit a double error. A limited nuclear war would in all probability destroy western Europe. A limited nuclear war would almost certainly become intercontinental and,

June 14, 1983
Supply
therefore, unlimited. For these reasons we here in Canada cannot suppose that this is a remote issue, remote from us. We are not armchair spectators watching in some disinterested fashion the tactics of the respective sides or pontificating from a limited base of knowledge. We have a role to play, and that role is to be found within NATO.
The policies that Canada advocates in the Council at NATO can do two things. They can take us closer to a nuclear war which would engulf this country among others, or the policies that we advocate within NATO can lead to a safer, more stable and perhaps ultimately non-nuclear environment in Europe. That would be vastly to our advantage. Nor should any of this surprise us, Sir. Twice alrealdy in this century Canadians have felt obliged to enter a war which began as a European conflict. The great difference now is that the nuclear tinderbox in Europe includes us, whether or not we wish to be included.
Given the immense gravity of this issue then, there is a broad path that I think we should take. On the one hand we must make sure that the immediate balance of forces is preserved so that the mutual deterrent continues to work in Europe as it has worked for almost 40 years. On the other hand, we must lend our weight to reversing the nuclear militarization of Europe even if this involves greater commitments to conventional weapons.
The 1979 decision of NATO of which, as Secretary of State for External Affairs I was a part, was quite compatible with this approach that I have outlined. At that time, as I remember, there was widespread concern in European countries about the Soviet deployment of SS-20 missiles and Backfire bombers in the western Soviet Union. There was a great deal of concern. The SS-20 missile, in particular, was seen directly to threaten the European members of NATO. There were no long-range theatre nuclear weapons held by NATO forces which could counter or offset the SS-20 missiles.
The vulnerability of our NATO partners-and it was expressed by so many of them in very direct terms-led us, that is the countries, of NATO to what has become known as the two-track decision. That decision meant, first, countering the SS-20 missiles and the Backfire bombers by deploying long range theatre nuclear weapons within the European countries of NATO, namely deploying the Pershing II and the Cruise missile. That was the first track of that two-track decision. Second, that decision meant seeking arms control negotiations with the Soviet Union to eliminate all long range theatre nuclear weapons from Europe, both East and West. Deployment was not to take place for four years. The decision reached was that there would be no deployment by NATO of these weapons for a four-year period, namely until December 1983 at the earliest. In the intervening period, the intention was to concentrate on the second track, to concentrate consistently and urgently on the arms control negotiations which would be carried out in Geneva.
One of the major concerns at that 1979 NATO ministerial meeting was to find a policy which would maintain the unity of NATO members. It was not easy; it was a very difficult search. Small countries of NATO, in particular, were not anxious to participate in a policy which would lead to arms escalation. The search for a consensus was indeed a difficult one. The Government of which I was a part agreed with the analysis of the imbalance in theatre nuclear forces in Europe at that time and it accepted that this imbalance had the very serious effect of potentially decoupling the American nuclear deterrent from the deterrents of nuclear war in Europe.
Our European partners in NATO were very concerned about this possibility. It bespoke volumes about their vulnerability to the SS-20 and the Backfire bombers with no guarantee that they could ultimately rely on the back-up of the American deterrent. The Canadian position at that time sought to allow European members of NATO to find their own consensus about the most appropriate response to the Soviet deployment of SS-20s. Clearly any NATO deployment would be on their territory, not in Canada. The deployment would be on the territory of western European countries. It was up to them to decide whether and how they wished to deploy these weapons.
Our concern at that time was not to strike any postures or to engage in rhetoric which might prejudice the ability of western Europeans to achieve a consensus. We should be quite clear, though, that throughout those meetings which resulted in the decision in 1979 at Brussels the decision in no way constituted a commitment by Canada to test the Cruise missile, nor was any such discussion entered into at the time of the NATO agreement. It never came up for discussion.
If we have an obligation now, it is because our attempt to find a common policy with our allies clearly imposes responsibilities, including co-operation in the testing of weapons systems which we have collectively agreed to deploy in western Europe should the arms control negotiations not be successful. Therefore, and specifically in regard to the Cruise missile, it is quite clear that our first and most urgent obligation is to use all our influence in the pursuit of an arms control agreement with the Soviet Union in Geneva. Anything else, including the testing of the guidance system of the Cruise missile, is secondary to the central issue of arms control. We must not allow ourselves to be deflected from the goal of arms control and reduction. That is what the 1979 decision of NATO was all about.
We should realize that today we have only six months left of the original four years which were agreed to to make progress toward an arms control agreement before deployment of the Cruise missile takes place in western Europe, six months left out of that four-year period. If the decision to deploy is implemented, if that is what we arrive at at the end of this year because the arms control negotiations have not been successful, then I feel we are obliged to share in the alliance effort which obviously will involve testing the guidance system of the
June 14, 1983

Cruise missile in Canada. But that obligation, related as it is to arms control negotiations, in no way required the Canadian Government to sign a bilateral agreement with the United States to test all manner of American weapons systems on Canadian territory. Yet that is the situation the Government created on February 10, 1983, when it signed the umbrella agreement with the U.S. That is the situation into which we have been put.
Under this new agreement or umbrella arrangement we have no guarantee that the weapons which are to be tested in Canada in the future will be part of our alliance commitments. They could equally be used for counterinsurgency in any part of the world, and the decisions could be made in secret, with no guarantee that Parliament will ever have the opportunity to debate the merits of these arrangements. All of this is being done by a Government which promised to suffocate the arms race in the laboratories. It is being done by a Government which has scarcely made any contribution to the discussion of arms control in Europe. Since the decision was taken in 1979, three and a half years have gone by and the Government has not yet been seized of the urgency of this situation. Surely it should realize that now is the time for Canada to take the initiative in an effort to move the negotiations forward. We should not underestimate our potential for doing so, nor our opportunity, nor indeed our responsibility.
If we look at the situation with regard to our other NATO colleagues, we realize it is extraordinary difficult for the British and the French to show flexibility because their nuclear forces are at the very heart or the centre of the dispute. For political reasons it is equally difficult for the West German Government to take the lead in the promotion of new ideas. If one looks at the political positions of the more junior members of NATO, one by one it becomes clear that there are precious few governments able to take initiatives and to introduce arms control proposals into public discussion. By contrast, Canada is in a position to test new ideas and to put into private and public discussion suggestions which may command some considerable support within the alliance. That is something we can do. As an interested and involved party, we should now be concentrating our efforts on presenting proposals to NATO which reflect both our own concerns and the political realities confronting our European allies, those I have mentioned.
We should begin not by engaging in a debate about the number of missiles on each side but by identifying some guiding principles. The Palme Commission suggested the notion of mutual security as the touchstone for negotiations with the Soviets. We should not, therefore, ignore the security dilemmas feed by the Soviets and we must realize the reality with which they live, namely that British and French or sea-based nuclear warheads are just as devastating as land-based warheads. Mutual security requires a formula and an approach which will deal with the Cruise and the SS-20 and will place them in the broader context of all medium range nuclear weapons currently targeted on both parts of Europe, East and West.
Supply
Our task as Canadians is to consider some of these possible solutions. It is well within the capacities of our experts to evaluate them and to explore the common ground of Washington and our European partners. To be rebuffed in this exercise will be disheartening. If we were to undertake it and be rebuffed, it would indeed be disheartening, but not to attempt it at all would be an abandonment of our role and our interest in the alliance. It would be to forget that there is still a place for genuine mediation within the alliance. It would be to assume that we in Canada have entirely lost influence and credibility with our closest friends. It would be to accept passivity and helplessness as the mark of our international diplomacy.
There are times when I am critical of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for some of his travels abroad, that they have not brought about the results that he or we might want to see. However, I would have no criticism, only commendation, if I could see the Prime Minister of this country engage in shuttle diplomacy from one country to the other in the western alliance to try to promote a much stronger effort by Canada for arms control negotiation in Geneva.
In this particular context, it is inappropriate to dwell upon specific numbers. Before we come to the precise arguments of the specialists, our task is to impose certain political principles on the negotiating process. Both in North America and in Europe there are hundreds of thousands of ordinary citizens who perhaps have seen more clearly than the scientists in defence laboratories and the strategists in the world of acronyms who know where present trends are leading us. We are faced with an apparently endless proliferation of nuclear weapons and destructive capabilities. Every new weapon has its own logic and its own reason, but the outcome is illogical, irrational and inhumane.
Therefore, and beginning with the INF negotiations Canada's approach to arms control should be guided by two broad principles. First, we must present realistic negotiating positions which emphasize minimal deployment of new weapon systems. We must begin to stem the tide of nuclear proliferation in Europe. Second, a negotiated outcome to the INF problem must encourage and actively promote further discussions on nuclear arms control.
In summary, the testing of the Cruise missile is not a decision which can or should be taken in isolation. Instead it must be placed, as I have argued, in the broader context of direction in arms control.
Finally, Canada must establish its own purposeful criteria for arms control and bend its efforts to achieving the only goal that in the long-term makes any sense, the progressive denuclearization of the world.
