subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 62-NON-CONFIDENCE MOTION-NUCLEAR WEAPONS TESTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take this opportunity to comment on a subject that has received a great deal of attention lately, and that is the testing of the Cruise missile in Canada. As all Hon. Members know, on February 10, 1983, Canada and the United States signed a five-year umbrella weapons testing agreement which established general ground rules for the testing of some of the U.S. military equipment and defence systems in Canada. At a later date, negotiators from both countries will try to establish a precise framework for the testing of different weapons, including the air-launched version of the Cruise missile in Alberta. However, to date no specific arrangement has been made to test Cruise missiles in Canada.
At the heart of the recent controversy is the Cruise missile itself, a missile which is basically a small, pilotless vehicle capable of delivering a nuclear warhead with great accuracy over long distances. It is too slow to be counted as a first strike weapon, but its accuracy and difficulty of detection makes it a devastating weapon. The Cruise missile is really the now generation of the V-l rocket the Germans developed near the
Supply
end of the Second World War that wrought such havoc on old London. The Cruise missile is very similar to that rocket except that it has wings and a guidance system. The Americans are not the only ones to have a Cruise missile. The Soviets, the French and the British also have similar vehicles, but only the Americans have developed the missile to such a high degree.
The U.S. is currently working on half a dozen different types of the Cruise missile. Most versions are being developed by the United States Navy and can be launched from submarines, surface ships or, in the case of the European version, by land. The other major type of Cruise is designed to be launched by B-52 bombers. This is the only type of Cruise that is presently being considered for operational testing in Canada.
The Cruise missiles have interchangeable roles. Almost every type of Cruise can be converted from nuclear to conventional warheads in relatively short order. They can also be outfitted to perform electronic warfare or surveillance roles. By making trade-offs with weapon payload, speed and fuel volume, the range of a Cruise can be extended from 370 miles to 1,500 miles without changing the missile's basic design.
Since Canada has foresworn the use of nuclear weapons on its own soil, it is already understood that none of the U.S. tests will involve nuclear warheads, nor will Canada be expected to deploy any of the missiles. The United States is expected to bear all testing costs. Also, there is a provision in the umbrella agreement which gives both countries the right to cancel or suspend any specific test. This gives us a great deal of control over the actual testing of weapons in Canada.
I think it is very important for Canadians to realize that we fully support NATO and the alliance. We believe that a credible deterrent is needed to maintain peace with liberty. That is why we supported NATO in 1979 when it adopted the "talk and deploy" or the two-track strategy. This strategy allows the western world to actively engage in negotiations that could contribute to meaningful and verifiable arms control and disarmament agreements, while at the same time to work with our allies to modernize our theatre and conventional defence forces in Europe so that they will in fact form a deterrent to the frightening build-up of Soviet armaments.
The military strategy of NATO, the strategy of flexible response, serves to preserve military security. Its aim is to prevent war through deterrence. Deterrence is effective when the allies are able to make credible their capability and willingness to defened themselves against any conceivable attack and can make the risk of attack unacceptable for a potential aggressor.
NATO is only capable of deterrence and defence through the close political and strategic co-ordination between North America and western Europe. Intercontinental strategic nuclear weapons, nuclear forces in Europe and conventional forces are required as deterrents for the entire spectrum of possible armed conflicts. NATO holds nuclear weapons at the ready not because it wants to wage a nuclear war, but rather because it wants to prevent war. The destructive power of

June 14, 1983
Supply
nuclear weapons is intended to deter the use of war as an instrument of policy.
Military security presupposes an approximate balance of military forces between East and West. Arms build-up alone, however, is not enough to provide certainty that a balance will remain stable and reliable in the long term. In order to attain lasting security, an attempt must be made to contribute to the creation of a stable military equilibrium at the lowest possible level by means of balanced limitations of military potentials.
Any efforts at obtaining quantitative and qualitative limitation and reduction of armaments must take into account the military efforts of the other side, especially existing imbalances in the ratio of military force, and must guarantee security in terms of defence capability at every stage of the process. Defence planning and arms control must be closely co-ordinated to preserve the capabilities necessary for the realization of this strategy. The defence and deterrent capability must be secured through the necessary military measures.
Deterrence is not an attractive way of ensuring peace, but at least it has worked. The maintenance of a credible deterrent has helped to make western Europe strong and to keep the peace for over 30 years, despite circumstances that were often difficult. That deterrent posture of the West still keeps the peace in Europe. To abandon our security system now in favour of alternatives that have not even been described coherently let alone thought through would be immensely dangerous. Deterrence also provides the necessary stability to enable us to negotiate international agreements on disarmament measures which will really give us a safer world if they are verifiable and apply equally to both sides. The possession of nuclear weapons is an essential fact of deterrence: in a world where such weapons exist the NATO alliance must be able to deter their use by an enemy or to resist blackmail based on the threat of nuclear attack.
At the same time, so long as there is no denying that it may fail, and it would be irresponsible not to have plans for trying to limit the damage once nuclear weapons are used. If the West is to remain dependent on the nuclear power of the United States, there is an obligation on us all to be constructive in our criticisms of United States policies, or at the very least to understand what they are trying to do. There is another obligation on which consensus appears to be developing on both sides of the Atlantic, that is, the need to improve conventional forces and so diminish reliance on nuclear weapons.
Canada participates in the nuclear strategies of NATO. However, our direct military contributions to alliance deterrence and defence lie in the defence by conventional means of land, air and maritime areas. This is not a question of morality. It is a question of how we can best contribute to our own security, given our limited resources and force size. But we cannot rationally condemn the possession of nuclear weapons by others in an alliance of which we are a member and in which nuclear weapons provide the basis of deterrence and
while we are sheltered by the deterrent nuclear umbrella of the United States or while we accept the contribution to deterrence and the prevention of war made by the nuclear forces of our British and French allies. To do so would be to adopt a position of no integrity whatever.
Canada's support for the maintenance of forces sufficient to deter aggression and defend the NATO area is entirely consistent with our commitment to a vigorous arms control policy. Indeed, the two policies are more than consistent, they complement and support each other, forming a coherent whole. They serve the same goal of enhancing security and preserving peace. Security is the key. Only on a basis of undiminished security can nations be expected to accept limitations on the numbers and quality of their weapons, and only on such a basis can they be brought to consider mutual and balanced reductions of their armed forces.
We are determined to do what we can to do what we can to achieve, by negotiation, a better international security environment. We are deeply involved in this effort. Canada not only encourages nuclear arms control between the two super powers, we also continue to seek mutual and balanced reductions in the conventional forces of NATO and the Warsaw Pact countries confronting each other in central Europe. These are negotiations that impact directly on the Canadian forces.
In addition to our participation in alliance consultations on strategic arms and intermediate-range nuclear force negotiations, our direct participation in the mutual and balanced force reduction talks and the conference on security and co-operation in Europe review process, Canada also plays a full role in the work of the United Nations and the Committee on Disarmament. Like other members of the United Nations, Canada is committed to the search for realistic and verifiable multilateral measures of arms control and disarmament which will halt the arms build-up. Canada's priorities in the United Nations are the achievement of a comprehensive multilateral nuclear test ban treaty, a chemical weapons convention, intended to complement the existing 1925 Geneva protocol and the 1972 bacteriological weapons convention, which would prohibit the development, production and stockpiling of all CW and provide for the destruction of existing stocks, and a treaty to prohibit the development, testing and deployment of all weapons for use in outer space. In all these areas Canada has made major contributions to the work being undertaken by the 40-nation Committee on Disarmament in Geneva.
The call by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) at the First United Nations Special Session on Disarmament, in 1978, UNSSOD 1, for a four-part strategy of suffocation and the unfolding of that strategy at UNSSOD II in 1982 into a policy of stabilization which took account of on-going negotiations, illustrates the contributions to the arms control and disarmament dialogue made by Canada in the past. We will continue our efforts in the future.
Several factors have contributed to the growth of antinuclear sentiment in Canada, many of which are common to other alliance countries. In part, it is a natural reflection of the
June 14, 1983

sharpening of East-West tensions following the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan and the uncertainties of the Polish situation. This has led in some quarters to a fear that war, particularly nuclear war, has become a real possibility. This has not been helped by various comments which were interpreted by some as implying that the U.S. was planning to fight a limited nuclear war in Europe. These fears have been heightened by recent nuclear defence decisions. NATO's INF modernization, in particular, continues to generate public controversy and opposition, which could grow in Europe especially as the time for the first deployment nears. The Government's decision to permit the testing in Canada of certain U.S. defence systems, particularly the Cruise missile, has added to public concern about nuclear weapons, and the debate in the U.S. over the MX strategic missile has also focused attention on the subject. The extensive media coverage given to these decisions has served to convince many that the nuclear arms race continues to escalate.
The conjunction of western decisions in the nuclear field and increased international tension has provided a natural impetus to the activities of the anti-nuclear lobby. A considerable amount of literature has appeared, much of it critical of nuclear weapons. Many of the arguments used by the antinuclear lobby are traceable to the Soviet propaganda campaign launched in 1979 to try to pre-empt the INF modernization decision.
The main themes of the anti-nuclear movement in part reflect the differing membership of the various organizations and in part the wider public concern about nuclear war. But the themes are relatively few, recur constantly in anti-nuclear literature and letters from the public and are concentrated on nuclear weapons issue specifically.
I personally support NATO's two-track policy and feel it is the safest route to follow at this time. To disarm unilaterally offers no protection against the bully who has expansionist tendencies and, in reality, would create a dangerous shift in the world balance of power. Indeed, it could rapidly lead to deterioration in relations between the super powers and a corresponding outbreak of another military confrontation.
For those of us who remember World War II, this position is all too clear. We can recall the disastrous appeasement policy of the allies in the pre-war days. The tragic results of this policy taught the free world that it does not pay to bow down before expansionist totalitarian powers. If we refuse to allow the testing of the Cruise in Canada by the U.S. then it will display to the Soviets that the western world is not united and will further erode the hopes for real, genuine negotiations on disarmament.
I am not suggesting that 1 am against disarmament; indeed 1 know of nobody in our country who would not favour disarmament. It is the ultimate goal that all mankind should strive to achieve. However, I do not feel this can be done by offering unilateral concessions. This tends to create imbalances, and at the very least leads to demands for more unilateral concessions. It is the path toward ultimate catastrophe. Surely we do
Supply
not want to return to that pre-World War II policy of appeasement.
In light of this I feel that we should proceed with the negotiations with the U.S. on testing the Cruise missiles. If an agreement is reached, Canada will be able to play a part in ensuring the strength and effectiveness of the NATO forces in maintenance of peace and security. However, if an arms control agreement is somehow reached between the Soviet Union and the West in the meantime, then the Cruise testing will be less urgent. If history teaches us anything, we would do well to remember that compromise and weakness did not prevent World War II. It nearly cost the western world its freedoms. Canadians as a whole support the strengthening of the NATO alliance believing that the best deterrence to war is to be prepared. The NATO countries dare not allow their military capabilities to become outdated. We watch with much anxiety the happenings in eastern Europe in recent years and in Afghanistan.
1 am confident that we will give serious consideration to any genuine Soviet proposals which would enhance the chance for effective and verifiable disarmament agreements. However, it is obvious that real progress can only be made on the basis of the principle of mutual security. I would like to remind all Canadians that the crux of the issue at hand is our own security, without which we are unlikely to continue to enjoy peace, independence, and hope. On this point we would all be well advised not to lose sight of these very important facts.

Members. We have reached the following agreement, which I would like to read to you.

The motion is rather short, but explicit; that following the disposal of the proceedings of the motion by the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent), the House shall consider the business of Supply as follows: first, opposed item in the Main Estimates, No. 8, provided that the same division shall apply to and be recorded on opposed item in the Main Estimates, No. 15, and opposed item in the Supplementary Estimates (A), No. 2; second, opposed item in the Main Estimates, No. 3, provided any division shall apply to and be recorded on opposed items in the Main Estimates, Nos. 4, 5, 10, 11, 12 and 21, and opposed items in the Supplementary Estimates (A), No. 1, and the motion for concurrence in the remaining Supplementary Estimates (A); third, opposed item in the Main

speechtext: Before we proceed to the vote on the Estimates, 1 would like to rule on certain of the Opposition notices. Notices Nos. 9 and 13 listed under the Main Estimates oppose statutory items.
